Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): I rise to a question of privilege arising out of an article published on the front page of the Vancouver Sun of Wednesday, March 8. The article reads:
Government May Get Rid of "Vocalamity".
That is a new word. I pronounce it differently from the way in which it is spelled because it sounds so bad when it is correctly pronounced.

subtopic: MB. POULIOT-ARTICLE IN VANCOUVER "SUN" OP MARCH 8
speechtext: Will the hon. member speak louder? We cannot hear him at all.

subtopic: MB. POULIOT-ARTICLE IN VANCOUVER "SUN" OP MARCH 8
speechtext:
Thank you. I continue with the quotation :
From the Vancouver Sun Ottawa Bureau.
Ottawa, March 8-Amid all the talk about parliamentary reform, a major step in that direction is being considered very quietly in Ottawa. The step is naming Jean Francois Pouliot, the too-talkative member from Temis-couata, to the Board of Transport Commissioners.
While observers say it would be a surprising appointment, the price might not be too great to pay for the ending of his lengthy speeches-
By the way, Mr. Speaker, I did not address the house since Thursday of last week.
-his bitter attacks on Defence Minister Ralston, and his criticisms of war expenditures.
He isn't just too talkative, he's "a vocalamity."
Accompanying the article is a picture of the person about whom it is written. Now, sir, may I make a brief answer. It is this. The writer of this article wants to cut the grass under the feet of the official press reporter of the senate. He wants to get the job of Tom Green in the senate. He is a nasty little fellow. For the rest, the article is perfectly untrue.

speechtext: I should like to mention to hon. members that on Sunday evening last the hon. I am glad to be able to say that I have been able to persuade the Minister of Finance to take a very much needed rest. It has been with the greatest difficulty that he has agreed to remain away from his official duties for a few weeks. I am sure that the house will share the feelings I have just expressed at the Minister of Finance having at last agreed to take this very much needed rest. No minister of the crown, I believe, has $yer given himself more completely to the duties of his office or has had more difficult problems to contend with than has the Minister of Finance since the beginning of the war. speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION OF CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
I wish to announce to hon. 
members that the Hon. Mr. Justice McTague has tendered his resignation as chairman of the national war labour board and the government has felt obliged, in the circumstances which have had to be considered, regretfully to accept Mr. McTague's resignation.
I should like to read the letters which have been exchanged between Mr. McTague and myself. I shall read first Mr. Justice McTague's letter to me:
Canada
National War Labour Board Ottawa,
March 8, 1944.
The Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, P.C.,	*
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
As I advised you in our conference of two weeks ago, I have made up my mind to resigD as chairman of the national war labour board. I have consulted the Minister of Labour and now ask you to accept the resignation as of March 17.
May I say, so that there will be no misunderstanding, my decision is not based on any differences with the government nor with the Minister of Labour personally. While the new wages order and the new labour code are perhaps not as I would personally devise them. I recognize the government's responsibility for them. As an administrator it is no function of mine to criticize. As a matter of fact I think the new code represents a milestone in labour relations and an excellent start. No doubt with experience amendments will prove necessary in both orders. That is to be expected in the natural course of things.
As I explained to you in conversation, I feel that what I set out to do on your invitation is completed to a point where someone else can now take over with a degree of confidence. The past year has been a particularly arduous one for me and I am rather tired. Besides I feel that I have been away from law too long. As you know I have spent more than three and one-half years in Ottawa on the work of the war contracts depreciation board and the national war labour board.
May I thank you personally and the other ministers for the manner in which you have all cooperated with me in my work. If some of fhy public statements have proved embarrassing at times I am sorry but I still think I must have been right.
Sincerely yours,
C. P. McTague.
My reply to Mr. Justice McTague is as follows:	It was written to-day.
Office of the Prime Minister
Ottawa, 16th March, 1944.
Hon. C. P. McTague,
Chairman, National War Labour Board,
Ottawa.
My dear Mr. Justice McTague:
I duly received your letter of the 8th of March, and have delayed its acknowledgment

Labour Relations Board
until to-day in the hope that you might find it possible to reconsider your decision and to continue as chairman of the board for at least a few months longer. From my conversations with you I understand fully the circumstances which have prompted your action, and which cause you to feel that you must adhere to the decision you had practically reached some little time before your letter was written. I have to-day communicated the contents of your letter to my colleagues in the cabinet. It is with regret that the government feels it should accede to your request and accept your resignation as chairman of the national war labour board.
I should like to take this opportunity to express anew the appreciation felt by the government of the signal service you have rendered to Canada's war effort in your capacity as chairman of the national war labour board throughout a very difficult year in the life of the board; also of the services you had previously rendered over a period of two and one-half years on the war contracts depreciation board.
I should like to add a word of warm personal appreciation of the uniformly lielpful and cordial relations which we have enjoyed during the whole of the period you have served as chairman of the board, and of your readiness throughout that time to be of such assistance to the government as lay within your power.
In the light of the strenuous nature of your duties I can well understand your present feelings of fatigue. I hope that being relieved of some of the pressure under which you have been working, you may speedily regain the resiliency of mind and spirit which in the past you have greatly enjoyed.
With kindest personal regards,
Yours sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King.
Mr. MaoINNIS: Has a successor to the Hon. Mr. Justice McTague been appointed, and, if not, will the functions of the board be continued in the meantime?

speechtext:
Hon. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour); I wish to announce that His Excellency the Governor in Council to-day approved of P.C. 1S95, establishing the wartime labour relations board for the purpose of administering the war-time labour relations regulations provided by P.C. 1003 of February 17 last. Mr. Justice G. B. O'Connor of the trials division of the Supreme Court of Alberta has been appointed chairman, and Mr. Justice J. N. Francoeur, of the Court of King's Bench of Quebec, vice-chairman.
The other members of the board are; Representing the employers, Mr. Harry Taylor,
Toronto; Mr. W. H. Brown, Toronto; Mr. A. Deschamps, Montreal, and Mr. A. J. Hills, Montreal. Representing employees are Mr. A. R. Mosher, Ottawa; Mr. W. L. Best, Ottawa ; Mr. Fred Molineux, Hamilton, and Mr. R. Harmegnies, St. Joseph di'Alma, Quebec. The representatives of the employers were selected after consultation with the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Construction Association, and the Railway Association of Canada. Mr. Taylor represents the manufacturers' association, Mr. Brown the chamber of commerce, Mr. Deschamps the construction association and Mr. Hills the railway association. The gentlemen representing labour were appointed after consultation with the four major labour organizations in Canada. Mr. Mosher represents the Canadian Congress of Labour; Mr. Molineux the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada; Mr. Best the railroad brotherhoods, and Mr. Harmegnies the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour. The members of this new board will meet shortly to organize and set up the machinery for the carrying out of their important work, which I sincerely feel will contribute in substantial measure to the creation of good relations between employers and employees in the Dominion of Canada.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition); I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister, of which I have given him notice. It has been intimated in the press that the Prime Minister of Australia plans to visit the United States within the very near future. Has an invitation been extended to Mr. Curtin asking him to include Canada in his itinerary? In the event of Mr. Curtin accepting such an invitation, can the Prime Minister give any information at the moment as to the approximate date of his visit to Canada?
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister); Some time ago, I extended the Right Hon. Mr. Curtin an invitation to visit Canada on his way to the meeting of prime ministers to be held in London at a forthcoming date. I am happy to say that in the reply received from Mr. Curtin he said he would be pleased indeed to visit Canada. At the time he was unable to say whether he would visit our country on his way to London or on his way back. I imagine Mr. Curtin may find it more convenient to pay his visit

on his return from the meeting overseas, when other matters may not be so pressing. I should like to say that it will mean very much to the government to have the opportunities of conference with Mr. Curtin on many matters of mutual interest to Australia and Canada, and I am sure the Canadian people will very much welcome a visit from Mr. Curtin.
I should like to add that if it is-possible for the Right Hon. Mr. Peter Fraser of New Zealand to pay another visit to Canada, either on his way to London or on his return, we should very much welcome such a visit on his part.
Speaking of the meeting of the prime ministers in London I was somewhat surprised to notice within the past day or two in one of the Canadian papers a lengthy statement to the effect that I myself might not be attending the meeting of premiers. From reading the article it was apparent to me it had been written for purposes of political mischief. I just w_ish to register a protest about statements of the kind being given publicity without my being given the opportunity of saying in advance whether or not there is any ground for such assertions. I mention this because I have noticed that there seems to be some new instrument at work in this country, which is continuously making references to matters which I am supposed to be doing, or that I am not going to do, most of which have no foundation at all. I should be pleased if those who attach importance to my doings or movements would, where the matters are important, kindly indicate a little in advance their intention to make public pronouncements and seek to ascertain the truth before inventing or spreading rumours.

This matter was raised earlier by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbnker) and I now raise it again at this time because of the republication yesterday in the Montreal Star of an article

Defence of Canada Regulations
written by Honorary Major C. W. Bailey, which appears in the Eighth Army News. This dispatch from the Italian front would indicate that the question is a live issue among the servicemen there, and would seem to merit a statement by the minister. If he is not in a position to answer to-day, perhaps he will do it at some other time.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO FURLOUGH FOR OVERSEAS PERSONNEL AFTER LONG SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, generally Your Honour has ruled that answers to questions such as these are not to be given immediately. However, I think this is a matter about which I might speak now, because I wish that there be no misapprehension with respect to it.
I say to the house and my hon. friend that the memorandum from the Royal Edmonton Regiment was received by me, and I might say that it is of a piece with the document I received some time ago from that same regiment in connection with the rehabilitation problem. It is a thoughtful and temperate document which is worthy of the traditions and the fine record of that very splendid regiment. It has had, and will continue to have, every attention.
The subject of leave for men overseas, it almost goes without saying, has had consideration steadily. As the leader of the opposition has said, it was mentioned by the hon. member for Lake Centre during the discussion of the war appropriation resolution. At that time, as reported at page 855 of Hansard, I said this:
I. am not in a position to make a statement on a matter of that kind, and the committee will understand why. Great events are pending and, if I took down correctly what my hon. friend said, he refers to a plan for rotating furloughs from certain areas and consideration being given to some foreign theatres. My hon. friend knows the location of our troops generally speaking, and I am not in a position to make an announcement of that kind to-night.
I can only add to that at this moment that operational conditions and shipping make it quite impracticable for me even to raise any hopes in this matter for the immediate or near future at least. I wish to add further that that does not mean that it will not continue to receive the attention it deserves, when changed conditions may warrant it. I should like to express the hope that nothing might be done which would indicate the possibility of favourable action at an early day. I think it is really only raising hopes which are not justified, and which possibly might create uneasiness at a time when we need steadiness perhaps as much as we have needed it at any time since the beginning of the War.

other members sitting, shall I say, in the more active area, or at all events the area where there seems to be perhaps more activity. I think we might perhaps all take a lesson from the fact that it is difficult for those at the far end to hear us. We who sit up here ought to make a personal resolution that we will speak so that we may be heard by those at the far end, no matter what the circumstances of the debate may be, and on behalf of those who sit with me on this side I suggest that that be done. I am sure that the Prime Minister will be only too glad to cooperate with me in this matter as he does in so many other matters-with perhaps some strange exceptions at times.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the statement which the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services has put on the record is just one more chapter of the achievements of the men of the armed services of this country. It is impossible to tell which has made the greater contribution, the men of the army, the navy, or the air force, but this is one more chapter of the achievements of the naval service.
The minister mentioned Royal Roads in his speech. I wonder whether he would give us a little more information on Royal Roads. How the the boys chosen who are sent to Royal Roads? Is there a quota from each province? Are they chosen on their scholastic records? Have they to make application for permission to enter Royal Roads?
I was glad to hear the minister praise the women of the armed services, especially of the naval division, and by the way I am glad to think that we have long since passed from naval defence to naval offence. I cannot see any reason, of course, why the women should not receive equal pay with the men. It should

War Appropriation-Naval Services
be the contribution that is made, rather than the sex, that determines the pay. However, the women of the naval service are glad to be serving. They are all volunteers and they serve gladly. But it is not only those who are in uniform who are serving. We should never forget that at home there are many who are serving for Canada just as much as the women in uniform. I refer to the women who are staying in their own homes, doing dull tasks sometimes, sometimes more pleasant ones-the women who are serving in the various societies that are sending comforts to the men overseas. I do not think there is a woman across the length and breadth of Canada who is not in touch in some way with a soldier, an airman or a naval man who is serving, either through their letters or through their efforts with the various organizations such as the I.O.D.E., the Red Cross, church organizations and auxiliaries, navy mothers and so on. The navy mothers are very active in my own city of Edmonton. AJ1 this work helps to keep up the morale not only of the men overseas but also here on the home front, which is also so important. t Alberta has 196 officers and 5,778 ratings in the naval service. That is a very good record, I think, for an inland province, and they are to be found in every branch of the service. There are those who are engaged in con\ oy work and others who are serving in the merchant marine. I think perhaps the convoy work is as important a work as any, taking the food and munitions and our men safely across the seas. It was a great triumph for the convoy system to bring down the number of ships sunk from one out of 181 in 1941, to one out of 233 in 1942, while in 1943 only one out of every 344 was lost. It shows how excellently our men have served.
I was glad to see the list of decorations for the naval service which the minister put on record on Monday. Five decorations were won by men from Edmonton, and I wonder if I nught be permitted to read the citation for just one of them. I read this particular one because it is first in alphabetical order in the list, beginning with "B". It is E. E Binnie Able Seaman, Royal Canadian Navy, who was decorated with the British Empire Medal on June 2, 1943. The citation reads:
. During prolonged engagements with U-boats a\i	attacks on convoys in the north
Atlantic, this rating performed his duty with certainty of precision which led to sight of U-boats on five occasions, thereby contributing to the saving of merchant ships.
That is only one citation out of many that might be given for devotion to duty and gallantry in action. There are, of course, [Mrs. Casselman.J
many who have given their lives in the service, and our sympathy goes out to their loved ones at home.
May I ask if it is the general principle that the men who are in training here in Canada are given a subsistence allowance rather than being provided with living quarters? If so, is the rate of subsistence for naval service the same as for the other services? When a man gets subsistence, is the rate the same here in Canada as it would be if his home base were abroad ?
I was glad to hear the minister's remarks about the cadet corps. It shows that our youth are very anxious to take their part as much as possible in actual positive work, and the training given is good not only for the service but also for citizenship here in Canada. Many of the leaders in this movement give freely of their time to this work.
Have many of the men of the naval service been taken prisoners of war, and is anything known about their treatment in camps? When they are able to escape and some marvellous stories of escape have come through is there any danger that the telling of these stories will make it more difficult for others to escape, or are there likely to be repercussions affecting those who help men to escape?
The frigate Stetler, I believe, is to be commissioned very soon. The minister will remember perhaps that the city of Edmonton did not have the honour of having a ship named after it for the reason that its name is so much like Edmundston in New Brunswick. However, the men of the town of Stetler have shown great bravery, and the Stetler is the ship which we claim as ours. I am sure that the men who serve on that ship will carry on the tradition of their fellows in the service up to the present time, and when they come back they will have a great work to do here, apart from the work they are doing abroad now for the building up of Canada.
I do not mean building entirely in the material sense. It is true that we need reconstruction and the development of our natural resources, but we also need citizens. Citizenship should mean something more than paying taxes and voting. It should mean something in the direction of building up the character of the country and the dignity of labour. A good citizen should contribute in more ways than materially.

As to the number of naval prisoners of war, I am glad to be able to say that it is very small. I believe the number is about six in all. I shall get the exact number presently. As to the prisoners of war who escape and who recount their stories, I think they are all careful net to say anything that might interfere with the safety of those who are left behind or who are likely to escape. They are careful not to give details regarding the route they followed or the manner in which they escaped.
As to subsistence, may I say to the hon. member for Edmonton East that the rate of subsistence in all points outside Canada is not necessarily the same as in Canada. Inasmuch as naval ratings are stationed at a great number of places outside Canada,-some in London, some in Washington, and some in St. John's, Newfoundland-I had better place on Hansard a table showing the different rates. For instance, in the United Kingdom, in the London area, a rating gets $2.25 subsistence whereas in Canada he gets only $1.25, and so on. In Washington there is another rate again. I think it would be well to put the complete list on Hansard for the information of my hon. friend.
The total number of prisoners of war I have given as six. It is nine-seven in German hands and two in Japanese.
The hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) asked a question as to the amount of naval material disposed of in the past year. Up to the present we have made no disposals through the newly instituted board under the Department of Munitions and Supply. We have disposed of certain goods under the former arrangement, through the salvage officer. I shall have to look up the record.

speechtext: Complaints have reached me regarding the length of leave granted to navy personnel who have served at sea' for some time. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
