maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister one or two questions about the naval situation on the Pacific coast in so far as Canada is concerned. Each of the ministers has made a brief reference to Canada's war policy on the Pacific. The Minister for Naval

War Appropriation

Naval Services
Services made his statement on Tuesday last in answer to a question of the hon. member for Yale which is found at page 1497 of Hansard. The minister said:
That question is covered by the general statement made by the Prime Minister, that we were all in the war together as united nations and would all pursue it to the end.
Then he went on to use these words:
The Canadian navy, I should think, would play a part in the war against Japan.
The minister gave much the same type of statement on March 9, which is found on page 1314, of Hansard, when he used these words referring to the personnel of our navy:
They are keen, of course, to get the war against Germany over, and then they feel that they have a few matters to attend to in the Pacific.
On March 6 the Minister of National Defence for Air made this statement in so far as his particular branch of the armed forces was concerned-it is to be found at page 1192 of Hansard:
Canada will be in the war against Japan until the very end. I am no strategist and cannot tell my hon. friend just what part we are going to take in the war on the Pacific, but we are going to shift from the European theatre to where we can do the most harm against Japan at the proper time.
The Minister of National Defence said on February. 14, to be found at page 466 of
IIansard:
In the first place, what I said with regard to Japan or what I wanted to say was, that no commitments have been made at the present time as to the nature or extent of Canada's participation in the war against Japan.
Hon. members of the committee will notice that each of these statements is indefinite. I think it can be assumed with accuracy that the policy of the present government is to leave the fighting against the Japanese in the meantime at least to the United States, Australia, New Zealand, Great Britain and possibly the Netherlands. Further, another branch of this policy is that the United States fleet is being relied on to defend Canada's Pacific coast, and, in the third place, it is the intention, I take it, that Canada will eventually participate in the war against Japan, when the war against Germany has been successfully concluded. I think that is a policy which requires careful consideration by the government and, frankly, a policy which requires revision.
May I emphasize these facts? Canada as a Pacific power should be taking part in the war against Japan now. As a Pacific power we cannot afford to stay out of the fight and allow those other nations to fight Japan for
us. If that is not to be our policy, certainly there can be no question that Canada should, at any rate, be carefully planning now what part she is to take in the war against Japan. I am afraid that the difficulty is that our staffs at Ottawa are thinking only of the war across the Atlantic. That has been the position from the start, ever since Japan struck at Pearl Harbor. Those of us who come from British Columbia had a difficult time in the winter and spring of 1941-42 prodding the government into taking action on the Pacific that would give us at least a reasonable defence against the Japanese on that coast. I repeat, I think the staff here, perhaps of the whole three forces, the navy, army and air force, is one-ocean minded. They do not realize that Canada is a two-ocean country-in fact we are now a three-ocean country. We are bounded by the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Arctic oceans.
I suggest that special preparation should be made now against the day when Canada really goes into the war with Japan. The British are doing that. I have here a press dispatch dealing with the speech of Sir James Greig, British Secretary for War, which was made in the House of Commons in Great Britain on March 2. In that speech he used these words:
In one field the ministry (of supply) can expect from us a whole range of new demands -those for specialized weapons and equipment which will be needed when we transfer our main weight to the war against Japan.
It is perfectly obvious that special equipment will be needed there along with special training. I do not think anybody can question it is a different type of war. Probably the fighting will be of an amphibious nature, landing from ships and seizing various islands, and naval fighting. Probably much of the fighting will be between the Japanese fleet and the American fleet, plus the British and the dominion fleets.
As I have said, Great Britain is preparing to take a very important part in the war against Japan. Her ships and troops are moving into that area. I have another press dispatch in my hand dated November 27, 1943. It states that the British navy is moving on to the Pacific coast of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Are they?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I want the minister to tell me.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows very well the answer to that question, I think.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I am hoping ter get an official answer from the minister. This dispatch says:
Vast expansion of naval base and repair facilities on the British Columbia coast, in preparation for the all-out drive against Japan, is foreshadowed in a statement by Admiral Sir Percy Noble, head of the British admiralty delegation at Washington, D.C.
Then the dispatch goes on to say:
Sir Percy declared that it is likely that the Royal Navy will-in its Pacific operations- seek permission to make use of Canadian bases. Such bases would undoubtedly remain under Canadian control. He considered it "unlikely" that separate bases would be operated by the Royal Navy.
Indications of increased naval activity on this coast in the near future are the recent presence of British and United States naval experts in Vancouver.
It has been reported, too, that Vancouver and Prince Rupert will share largely in the activity to come.
Our own admiral on the Pacific, Admiral Brodeur, is reported: in the press of December 3 last to much the same effect. He is quoted as saying:
There is no doubt in my mind that Vancouver and Victoria will be used in case of large naval operations for the repair of ships. There are bound to be a few damaged ones.
The newspaper report goes on to say:
Asked whether the Royal Canadian Navy would- operate with the Royal Navy, Admiral Brodeur pointed out that such action has been a matter of long-standing policy with both services, and said the R.C.N. "will play a very big part when the 'first class second front' begins."
The position is that the first thing we know, if Canada does not take her fair share in the war against Japan, she will be left out of the decisions that will be made after the war with regard to all the lands lying around the Pacific ocean. Only to-day the Prime Minister referred to the agreement between Australia and New Zealand which was negotiated late in January; he pointed out that he thought it was a very important agreement. Incidentally the Australians and New Zealanders have asked Canada to become a party to that agreement. These specific questions must be faced by the Canadian government; they must not be pushed aside to be dealt with "if" or "perhaps", after the war with Germany is ended. Canada, as a Pacific power, must have a fair share in the decisions which will be made after the war as to the future in the Pacific.
I suggest that the members of this committee and the Canadian people are entitled to know what part the Canadian navy is going to play in the war against Japan and also what is the Pacific policy of the present government. We should have that in far more

detail than the general statement made by the minister to this effect: "The Canadian navy, I should think, would play a part in the war against Japan." Then we are entitled to know whether or not Great Britain has sought permission from Canada to use naval bases on our Pacific coast and, if that permission has been sought, whether or not Canada is granting it, and also whether the Canadian Navy is cooperating fully with the Royal Navy on the Pacific coast. . I have no doubt that will be done if it is left to the personnel of the Canadian Navy. We are entitled to be reassured on this whole question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
While I appreciate what has been said by the hon. and gallant member for Vancouver South with regard to the great Pacific question, Canada is now bound by the arrangements made between Mr. Churchill and the President of the United States at Cairo and the other conferences which have been held. As you know, Mr. Chairman, both before and after Pearl Harbor Great Britain had practically left the Pacific, which was looked upon as the exclusive preserve of the United States. Great Britain was not ready for war. After Hong Kong and Singapore fell we found that commitments and preferences had been made, to the effect that Britain was not able to take charge of the war on the seven seas; she had not the fleet, owing to disarmament on land, sea and in the air. So as a result of the conferences that were held, by which Canada is bound as a member of the British empire, the Pacific war came to be looked upon as the particular allotment of the United States.
What has happened? You have all seen what has taken place in the Pacific, which I spoke gbout before Pearl Harbor, when I saw the war coming. I said that the Japanese, who were our allies in the last war, would be island-hopping around to all the ten thousand miles of islands in the Pacific, and that is what they have been doing. They have appeared in all those islands, and they are all mined, we have the gravest possible state of affairs in that particular campaign. What happened at the Cairo conference, to which Canada was a party? Mr. Churchill and the President of the United States made commitments with regard to the Pacific. What are those commitments to which Canada has agreed? Canada, by Cairo, has agreed that Japan must give up all the territories it has acquired in the last fifty years, and as well must give back everything she has conquered since Pearl Harbor. Well, it seems to me, and we do not even yet appreciate it, that the war with Japan will last another four years, and I am

War Appropriation-Naval Services
afraid that sooner or later the allies will have to agree not to go as far as they went at the Cairo conference, which by the way has been criticized very strongly in the British press and house. Certain commitments have been made since the war started; some are primary, such as aid to Russia, and others are secondary. The defeat of Germany is the most important thing of all, and Canada should keep out of the Pacific until she has a fleet strong enough to play its part in that campaign. After all, the mother country is in this war against Japan on land, sea and in the air.
As I said the other night, the Canadian navy has played a glorious part in the war so far, but we have not yet the ships or the men to play a very active part in the Pacific at the present time. That theatre of war has been left pretty much to New Zealand, Australia and the United States; and the contribution that has been made by the splendid United States forces and by Australia and New Zealand is most praiseworthy. It is true that after Hong Kong and the rout at Singapore Canada sent a number of men to Iviska, where they did splendid work. It is also true, as the minister said the other night, that we have done a good deal in connection with the development of harbour facilities there; but as I said in 1936 and 1937, speaking from this side of the house, from Puget Sound for six hundred miles through the Queen Charlotte islands we had at the Pacific an undefended coast line which was just inviting trouble, absolutelj' unprotected, through the policy of this country in not having a proper fleet or any proper form of defence. British Columbia is entitled to everything we can give her; I am very sorry it has been necessary to have blackouts there and all that sort of thing, but I do not see what we can do at the present time. The government is bound by the arrangement that has been made, giving the United States the prerogative in the Pacific, which we abandoned after the Singapore base was lost.
Back in 1937, when the Japanese question was under discussion, the present Minister of Pensions and National Health, who was then Minister of National Defence, did manage to get some increases in the estimates in regard to the Pacific coast. At that time I pointed out that 630 miles of that territory was unprotected ; that it had hundreds of inlets and harbours, but we had no fleet to guard it. The minister brought down a return showing the size of our navy, which consisted of two or three destroyers, I believe, totalling less than ten thousand tons in all. It was not the fault of anyone, as far as I can see, because they were all pacifists, both in and out of this 100-96
house. I know I was accused of being a warmonger away back on March 24, 1938, five months before Munich, when I pointed out the grave danger in the Pacific, as well as the dangers over in Europe.
I appreciate the position of the hon. member for Vancouver South, the hon. member for Vancouver North and all the members from British Columbia, who have been most active in the interests of their province, but we must face the facts. The mother country had no fleet left; she threw away her defences and depended on Geneva up to the time the war broke out. Blame the pacifists who brought about this state of affairs after Britain had ruled the seas for a hundred or more years. We had peace for a hundred years from 1815 up to the time of the last war, except for a little outbreak in 1900. Britain had supremacy on the seas, together with commercial supremacy; and when you lose that you cannot get it back in a day, a month or a generation. I think the minister was quite right in what he said the other evening, that the war with Germany was primary, and I believe the government is quite right in its Pacific policy, until such time as Germany is beaten, and dear knows she is far from beaten yet. Where are you going to get a fleet to operate in the Pacific? Can you take it out of the Atlantic, the North sea, the Mediterranean and the Indian ocean at the present time?
We had a little experience in Kiska. I can tell you this, that we do not want any more Hong Kongs in the Pacific, or any of that kind of thing. With all the tipping off that has been going on, until we are ready we do not want to send troops, air force' or forces of the army to the Pacific area, to those numerous islands which are all mined. Look at the loss of life the United States has suffered in the glorious work it has done. Look at the awful loss in the United States fleet in the Pacific, and in their air and land forces. Do not forget the great debt of gratitude we as a dominion owe to New Zealand and Australia. Before the war started they gave to maritime freedom in the Pacific $5,000,000 a year to the Singapore base. That base was lost by bad management, by the infiltration of infantry, and the lack of forethought.
Until we know that Germany is beaten I cannot see how we can put up a fight against Japan-we a people of only 10,000,000. people. We have not the armaments to do it. The main thing is to see that Germany is defeated and, as Mr. Churchill has said, when Germany is defeated all the power of the mother country will be placed behind the United States



War Appropriation-Naval Services
to destroy Japan, that awful race which has acted as cannibals toward our soldiers overseas.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: May I have an answer to my question?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
With regard to the use of bases on the Pacific by the British navy, my hon. friend wanted to know whether the United1 Kingdom had asked permission to use those bases, and if so whether such permission had been granted. By the agreement of 1910, when Great Britain abandoned her bases in Canada, and when they were taken over by the dominion, there was a clause to the effect that the British government should always have the right, or that His Majesty's ships should always have the right, to use the bases both at Halifax and Esquimalt, free of any charge, with the exception of charges for labour and materials, which those ships would have to bear.
Then, as to whether Canada should take part in the war against Japan:	I believe my
hon. friend made the same plea last year with regard to land forces of Canada. He pointed out that Canada should take part in that war, and I think he indicated that a contingent of land troops should go into the war against Japan. He now makes the same request with respect to naval forces. I am not speaking unkindly when I say that there have been a great many suggestions as to how the Canadian Navy should be disposed. Many suggestions have been made since the beginning of the war, some m the house, some by newspapers outside the house, and others on public platforms. We had a remarkable number of such suggestions in 1942. Some people thought we should take [DOT] the whole Canadian Navy and defend the gulf of St. Lawrence only, or the strait of Belle Isle, or Cabot strait. That, they thought, was the entire function of the Canadian Navy. Those entrusted with the strategic direction of the navy said no; that that was a ridiculous naval policy, and that no navy worthy of the name would1 adopt a policy of that kind-sitting back on its own shores, waiting to be attacked. They pointed out that the thing to do was to go out and meet the enemy as far away from our own coast as possible, and to endeavour to defeat him there.
That policy was adhered to in the face of strong and bitter criticism from certain quarters in Canada. It was adhered to, and it bore results, because in 1943 not a single German submarine made an attack in our coastal waters. Why? Because they were being attacked themselves out in mid-Atlantic,

and they are being attacked almost at this very moment in mid-Atlantic. Some of them are being sunk by Canadian ships of war. That was the policy we pursued then, and we w'ere right.
With regard to the Pacific, and the sending of our naval forces to that area, I would point out to my hon. friend that the sea is one. That is an old and very true naval maxim. My theory is that anything done in one part of the sea against the enemy may be taken to be done in all parts. If you destroy an enemy submarine in mid-Atlantic you weaken the general power of the enemy. When they sank the Schamhorst off the north tip of Norway about the end of the year, that was a blow at the entire axis sea power. When a few days later two cruisers, one of which was commanded by a Canadian officer, sank four German destroyers in the bay of Biscay, that too was a blow at axis naval power.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
But the bulk of axis sea
power is in the Japanese fleet, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Probably it is, although the German submarine fleet, I think, is more powerful than the Japanese.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Not more powerful than the Japanese fleet, surely?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I
was speaking of the submarine fleet. I think the German submarine fleet is more powerful than the Japanese. The Japanese fleet of course has more surface vessels. But the point is that the fact that we have not many ships actually in Pacific waters at the present time does not mean that we are not assisting in the battle of the Pacific. By no means does it mean that. For instance, how much assistance is Great Britain giving with respect to the war in the Pacific at the present time? How many units of the British fleet are in the Pacific? But will my hon. friend say for one moment that Great Britain will not have a voice at the peace table so far as the Pacific possessions of axis powers are concerned, merely because the bulk of her fleet is elsewhere at the present time? Does my hon. friend say that Russia will have a lesser voice in peace discussions because she has no fleet in the Pacific?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The British have had units
of their fleet in the Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
As
the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) pointed out, the strategy of this war to a great extent was to leave the Pacific very largely to the Americans, to leave the Atlantic to the British fleet, and the convoy work to the

War Appropriation-Naval Services
British and Canadian fleets. That was the general arrangement made, and it has worked out with reasonable satisfaction.
I cannot undertake, even if I knew, to give my hon. friend the exact number of ships in the Pacific, either Canadian, British or American.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I did not ask for that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I
cannot attempt to do it. And I do not think I can amplify the statement I made the other day, that it is the intention, as announced by the Prime Minister, that Canada shall have a part in the Pacific war. I have no doubt that the Canadian navy, the Canadian air force and the Canadian army will take part in it. Beyond that I cannot go. I do not take that stand with any intention whatsoever of disregarding our great coast which faces the Pacific, or the importance of the ports in British Columbia.
We are disposing our fleet to the very best possible advantage, in accordance with 'the plan agreed upon by all those vitally concerned-Canada, the United States and Great Britain. And in view of impending events in Europe, which I need not discuss at the present time, in view of their importance, and in view of the part Canada is going to play, and play on the sea, in those events, I say it would be very difficult for us to do anything different from what we are doing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is any thought being given to plans for the Canadian Navy in the Pacific, once Germany is beaten? Is there any special planning being done, or any special training being carried out for the type of warfare which will be followed in the Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
As I said the other night when speaking with regard to rehabilitation, some people think we should be devoting our whole time to consideration of post-war problems. As I said last week it is my view, and I am proud to say it is the view of the personnel of the Canadian Navy, that our great concern is: Let us win this war first. I say of course that we are giving some thought to after the war. But let us get the war over first. We have a job to do as a navy, and we are doing it, and doing it successfully. While we have that job to do I do not know that we can spend too much time in sending ships to the Pacific to study methods of warfare in that area. [DOT]
All our staffs are constantly endeavouring to keep up to date with the progress of the war in the different theatres of war. They are endeavouring to follow the new types of warfare being developed at sea, on land and in 100-96i
the air. And our naval staff is not at all remiss in that regard. But when my hon. friend asks me if we will send ships to the far Pacific, to the southwest Pacific-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I did not ask that at all. The minister cannot put words into my mouth like that. I do not suppose he wishes to be unfair, but I did ask him whether he has any branch of his naval staff, or whether he has any officers or others doing special planning work for the Pacific. I am not questioning the good work that is being done by the navy in the Atlantic. It is unfair to drag a red herring across the trail in that way. I am asking whether there is any planning being done in regard to Canada's part in the naval war on the Pacific. Surely there are enough personnel in the navy now for some at least of them to be put on that job.
Mr, MACDONALD (Kingston City): The department of plans of the navy and the naval staff are giving attention to all matters of this kind. I say again that we cannot do a hundred things at once. You cannot fight on the Atlantic and on the Pacific too with the same ships. My hon. friend ought to realize that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I did not suggest anything of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Let me ask my hon. friend, does he say that we should take one-quarter or one-third of our forces in the Atlantic and send them to the Pacific, or what proportion?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I did not say that at all.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Give me a figure. He thinks we can take part in the Pacific war. I ask him, to what extent should we do that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Calm down!

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
He cannot calm down. I suggest to the minister that there should be on the naval staff right now, and there should have been for a long time, somebody whose job was to make plans in regard to Canada's part in the naval war on the Pacific. I did not suggest that one ship or ten ships should be moved or anything of that kind. I do say this to the minister, that if Canada does not watch out and pay a little more attention to the war on the Pacific she will seriously endanger her relationships with Australia and New Zealand and possibly with the United States. We are a Pacific nation and it is part of our job to prepare for participating in the war on the Pacific.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
My hon. friend is changing his stand considerably, because he started out by saying that Canada should take part in the war in the Pacific, and I understood him to say that we should send ships to the Pacific. I ask him where he thinks we would get them, and where should we take them from? Does he suggest in view of what is going to happen in Europe that we should take ships out of the Atlantic? I can tell my hon. friend that we are going to take part in that action against the continent of Europe. Canadian forces, land and sea and air, wall take part in that invasion in no small measure. Would he say that we should jeopardize the success of that invasion by taking ships from there? Should we take them out of the convoy service to Europe, where we are already doing 40 per cent of the convoy wrork now? In addition, a large part of the north Atlantic is entirely under the command of Canadian naval officers. Does he think that we should take ships out of there? If he sa3's no, then I ask him where are we 'going to get the ships to send to the Pacific?
As I have already said, there is a plans branch in the department and we have a naval staff which is giving attention to the Pacific war as it is to all types of sea warfare. Beyond that I cannot go.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Why did not the minister say that ten minutes ago?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I did say before my hon. friend rose that we had a plans branch and a naval staff that were always studying naval warfare. They are studying the Japanese war and Japanese methods. But my hon. friend was asking us to send ships to the Pacific just as last year he wanted a contingent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There are already ships in the Pacific, as the minister knows.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Does my, hon. friend want us to withdraw those ships from those waters?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am
prompted to speak after listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Durham a couple of days ago describing the enthusiasm of the people of Port Hope because a ship of the Canadian navy had been named after Port Hope. It recalled to my mind that in the early days of the war some of the citizens of the town of Pembroke, the county town of Renfrew county, had asked me if it might not be possible to have a ship named after the

town of Pembroke. I wrote to the department of naval service, and we were disappointed to get a reply that that was not possible as there was already a ship by that name in the British service.
But as I listened to the hon. member for Durham the other night, it occurred to me that perhaps there would be no objection to naming a ship after the township of Wilber-force. Wilberforce is not a city or town; it is a township of lakes, splendid scenery, some very good fanning country, and many good farm homes maintained by hard-working ambitious farmers. While it may have no great claim to fame, it has perhaps some little claim for special notice in that it has contributed its fair share of men to public service in this country. Doctor Maloney, who was elected to this house as a member of parliament for South Renfrew on three occasions, was bom and raised in the township of Wilberforce. The late Alexander Stewart, who spent his life time in the township of Wilberforce, was elected on two occasions to represent North Renfrew in the Ontario legislature. Stanley Hunt, who was elected to represent North Renfrew in the Ontario legislature at the last election, was born and raised in the township of Wilberforce. I have myself spent my lifetime in the township of Wilberforce, and North Renfrew has done me the honour of choosing me to represent them for one term in the Ontario legislature and on two occasions they have elected me to represent them in this house. I would therefore ask the minister if it would not be possible for him to consider having a Canadian ship named Wilberforce.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Will the minister give a reply to the remarks made by Sir Percy Noble, followed by Admiral Brodeur, with regard to the use of facilities on the Canadian Pacific coast for the British fleet? He did refer to the old agreement of many years ago with regard to the facilities then existent, but as I read the remarks of Sir Percy Noble they were extremely definite that it was intended to quarter ships on that part of the coast, and Admiral Brodeur was of the same opinion. But from the minister's reply to the hon. member for Vancouver South it sounded as if there were nothing in it. Would the minister say there was nothing in it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I would not say there was anything in it or nothing in it. All I say is that if the British wish to make use of the base at Esquimalt for their ships they are at perfect liberty to use it under the agreement of thirty or more years ago. As to British Columbia ports being made

War Appropriation-Naval Services
a base for a large section of the British fleet in the war against Japan, if Sir Percy Noble made such a statement-I have not got it here -I assume that he was speaking with due deliberation and it may thus be assumed that he was speaking correctly. But I cannot add to or take anything away from his statement. That is all I can say. I know of no plans involving the use of Pacific ports by the British fleet beyond the old agreement of thirty years ago.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The implication in Sir Percy Noble's remarks was undoubtedly that Canadian ships being extremely busy on the Atlantic side it was the intention of the government-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The British government?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I presume he would not have made that statement had the idea had not had the acquiescence of the Canadian government, and I am surprised to hear the minister say that so far as he is aware no such pronouncement is accurately made.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There is very little definite about the Pacific war except, as I said the other day and have said repeatedly, that we are planning to take part in that war. I have no doubt that the British fleet will take part in that war, but in exactly what way is another story. On that point I can give my hon. friend no information at all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
A few days ago when the minister was asked as to the type and size of vessels for a permanent Canadian navy he indicated, as I understood him, that this was a matter that should be left until the war was over and that it would depend on the urgency and particular needs of the times. I am one of those in this house, and have been and will continue to be who are in favour of Canada, having a substantial permanent navy. I believe that Canada needs a navy, and if Canada is to be a great country it needs a navy particularly from the standpoint of defending its shores and taking part in any combat in which it sees fit to engage. That brings up the question, and that is why I speak about it to-day, of maintenance and repair facilities, plans and personnel. If it is suggested that I am too realistic, I reply that we have to look at what is going to happen in connection with our repair yards and shipbuilding facilities when the war ends.
May I state my view in a few words. As soon as the war ends the cargo shipbuilding programme will cease and our naval shipbuilding programme will in a large measure
be discontinued. It will be found that shipbuilding and ship repairing facilities will decline in consequence. It appears to me, therefore, that some thought should be given to the maintenance of repair facilities in order to look after naval ships when the war is over and to keep them in proper condition. We should also have trained workmen available at all times for the purpose. Unless some plan is made in that regard we shall be faced with a lack of proper facilities as well as of the workmen who will be needed when the time comes. The minister should keep in mind the present facilities that have been set up on the Atlantic coast. The maritime ports are available twelve months of the year and the facilities that are there now should be kept up so as to fill the need which will make itself felt in the future. Unless this is done we shall find, if Canada is ever faced with the situation that existed in 1939, that it will be necessary for us to build all over again and it may be two or three years before we can recover the position we held at the present time. I hope that the planning departments under the minister are giving some thought to this matter, that they will approve the idea of retaining the facilities we have now and our ships as well and of keeping them in as good condition as they are in at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The hon. member for Peterborough West asked for the number of civil servants taken on during the past year. The number is 545, both here and at outside points.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: In the return tabled on March 3 it appears that seventy of these men are in Newfoundland. How many civil employees have we there altogether, and how. many are in Britain- or are there any there?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I will . get that information in a moment as regards Newfoundland. The number serving in the United Kingdom, is eight.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The return shows that there were seventy added in Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is quite possible. There is a considerable expansion in St. John's, Newfoundland, and it may be that seventy were taken on since August of last year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The minister repeated a few moments ago the very same statement he made the other day, namely, that there were certain short-sighted people in 1942 who were

War Appropriation-Naval Services
asking that the whole Canadian navy be moved into the gulf of St. Lawrence to deal with the * submarine menace there. I suggest that he is magnifying the fact a bit when he says that people asked for the whole Canadian navy to be sent there. I am not aware that any person or any newspaper ever asked that the whole navy be moved to that locality. What people and the newspapers asked was that some protection should be given our ships there. The minister goes on to say that the policy of his department was a wise one, that by fighting the submarines on the open sea we took the best means of destroying and getting rid of them. I wonder if the submarines could not have been got at and destroyed more easily in the St. Lawrence. If they could have been got rid of in that locality would not that have served the end as well as fighting them outside,? But that is not all. If the minister's policy was the right one, and if in 1943 we did not have any submarines in that section by reason of the fact that his department followed the right policy the year before, how is it that the government made provision for such effective defence of the Gaspe coast last year? The defence organization was widely advertised throughout the Canadian press last summer. Every hon. member must recall the kind of publicity that was given the organization that was established on that coast last year. As a matter of fact, we had a very good organization last year and that may explain in part why we had no [DOT] submarines then. Well, if it was advisable to fight the submarines in 1942 on the high seas, because that was the best way to destroy them, I should like to know, assuming that it was useless for short-sighted people to ask for some protection in the St. Lawrence, why the government has set up such admirable protective safeguards as those we have now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I suppose a submarine could be sunk in the gulf or the river St. Lawrence as well as anywhere else. There is no doubt about that. But I must leave to the naval staff rather than to my hon. friend the task of determining how the navy should be disposed of to the best advantage. They disposed of it as they thought best in 1942. There were naval ships in the gulf and the river St. Lawrence all the time in 1942, and there were others on the high seas. Submarines did not attack in the gulf of St. Lawrence last year. I am sure that if they had done so, the civilian defence corps, which my hon. friend speaks of, would have been helpful in spotting and reporting them, but I cannot think that the civilian defence corps kept the submarines away from the gulf.
OSr. Roy.]

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am not talking only about the civilian defence corps on the coast; I am referring to the number of ships we have had in Gaspe harbour. Moreover, we have had planes and telephone lines and all the other organization that has been set up. We had more ships and planes last year than the year before.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Of course we had more ships and planes last year than in 1942. We have added considerably tc the strength of the navy and air force anc consequently we had more ships for mid Atlantic and the gulf of St. Lawrence. My hon. friend is quite right about that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: May I say a word, which has been prompted by the debate that took place a few moments ago in which the hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for Gaspe took part. I can recall the debate that occurred in the last session when I came to the rescue-or rather to the support, shall I say, since he did not need to be rescued-of the hon. member for Gaspe, when he made certain suggestions with regard to strengthening the position on the east coast from the point of view of submarines. I should not like to think the minister is not susceptible to suggestions from any part of the committee, but in that particular instance it seemed to me that when the hon. member for Gaspe did come forward with suggestions they were not welcomed in the manner I should like to have seen. I hope that the inquiries which are being made by the hon. member for Vancouver South will not be found in the future to be in the same category. Perhaps the minister may find that there is something with respect to the position on the west coast that has a similar bearing to that which was brought to the attention of the ministry last year by the hon. member for Gaspe. I should like to think the minister is prepared to give careful and keen consideration to the suggestions and inquiries brought forth honestly and in a desire to help by members of this committee. On reflection I think he will not want to deal with the hon. member for Vancouver South in the way that he did this afternoon. I think all the hon. members of this committee, regardless of party affiliation, are anxious to try to be as helpful as they possibly can; otherwise the debate and the appropriations and the opportunities given to discuss them become, of course, of limited importance.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
In answer to my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, the only thing I wish to say to the committee is this: I cannot attempt to give the detailed disposition of ships, whether
MARCH 16, 1944	[DOT]	1527
War Appropriation-Naval Services
it be in the Pacific or in the gulf of St. Lawrence or in the Atlantic. It simply cannot be done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Nobody was asking that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: If anybody asks me how many ships there are, here or there, I cannot attempt to answer such questions. I do not think they should be asked. I do not say my hon. friend from Vancouver South was endeavouring to put his question as pointedly as that, but I think my hon. friend himself knows, for instance, how many British ships are in Vancouver at this time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I do not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I thought there was nothing that I could tell him which he did not pretty well know already.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The minister is quite wrong there.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I shall be glad to tell my hon. friend anything I can.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am prepared to accept the explanations made by the minister when they are reasonable. But since the year 1942 has been mentioned by the minister, may I say I do not like to be called a traitor or shortsighted. I think the minister would do well to desist from giving expression to such remarks in the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I never suggested that my hon. friend was a traitor or anything of the kind. My hon. friend is mistaken if he assumes I ever intimated that he was anything of the sort.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
In opening his discussion on these estimates the minister said that during the next fiscal year the navy planned to take in personnel to a number of about 12,000. That is half the number required during the present fiscal year. I presume that there is quite a large wastage, quite a few men are discharged each year. Will the minister tell us whether or not those 12,000 men will simply maintain the navy at its present strength of 80,000 or whether the establishment is to be increased?
It has been announced that the Canadian Navy is now to be a fleet with large ships. In other words, it is no longer to be what the minister described as a small-ship navy. Perhaps we are all in [DOT] agreement with the change in policy. I am glad those heavier ships are being acquired, but there is considerable uncertainty as to the government
policy with regard to a merchant navy. I take it that in peace time the principal job of our navy will be to protect our shipping. Some one or another of the ministers should explain the policy of the government with regard to a merchant navy. Admiral Brodeur said on November 24, 1943:
It is incorrect to think that a strong sea power can be obtained by building a strong fighting navy alone. To have real sea power a nation must also have a strong merchant navy.
Last December the Minister of Munitions and Supply advocated Canada having a proper merchant fleet. He said:
Canada should provide a merchant marine worthy of the dominion's export position.
Two weeks later the Minister of Transport said that he could see no future in Canada going into the shipping business on a big scale after the war. He went on to point out the difficulties of keeping up a merchant navy. Is the minister in a position to state to-day the policy of the government with regard to a merchant navy? It is of the utmost importance to the whole of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am not in a position, because, while it was suggested the other night by the hon. member for Cape Breton South that the merchant navy be put in uniform and made part of the service navy, that has not been done in this country or in Great Britain. The merchant navy is a totally distinct branch from the service navy. I really have nothing to do with the merchant navy beyond the general interest that I hope every Canadian has in the establishment of a strong mercantile marine.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The minister is not in a position to state the policy of the government with regard to a merchant navy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
No, I am not.
My hon. friend asked if the complement of the Canadian Navy would be increased during the year. I may say it will. The total complement at the end of the fiscal year will be, we hope, about 12,000 men more than it was at the beginning of the fiscal year, allowing for discharges and casualties.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
There are a few matters I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. One of them is a year old and I have not as yet received an answer to it. It has to do with the establishment of an insurance scheme for the armed forces. I am not going into details in connection with it. I did that on June 9, 1943. I then set out the particulars of the scheme in effect in the

War Appropriation-Naval Services
United States. Under that scheme some 7,750,000 servicemen in the various armed services of that country had made application for insurance under the system in effect there. Under that system insurance is available for S6.70 a month per SI,000 of insurance. If a similar system is adopted in Canada, those who serve will be able to build up a nest-egg when they return, and if they do not return then those nearest and dearest to them will be assured of a monthly payment over a period of fifteen years on the basis of a $10,000 policy. The amount paid per month is, I believe, approximately $50. When I asked the minister a question last year on this matter he stated that he would take it up with the other ministers for defence and in due course would give an answer. Without going into the particulars to-day, I now ask him whether or not it was taken up; whether the decision of the Canadian government is that it will not bring into effect a system of insurance for the armed services in order to place those who serve in the Canadian army in the same position as are the men who serve in the United States army.
Then there is one other matter. As far as the other armed services are concerned we find to-day many young men who for a period of four or five years since the beginning of the war have been in the armed services, but prior to that time had not been. They have achieved senior ranks to-day. Men who in 1939 ranked as lieutenants or captains command divisions to-day. In the air force the same situation prevails. I think of a young man in my own constituency who was mentioned in the press to-night, Wing Commander Robert Turnbull, D.F.C., A.F.C. In a period of nine months of service he rose from the rank of sergeant-pilot to wing commander, one of the most distinguished records in the Royal Canadian Air Force overseas.
As far as the navy is concerned I have heard it said on many occasions that men from the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve are, by the operation of things, denied the opportunity of promotion to the senior ranks. I know it will be said that the position is different in the navy from that in the army or the air force. But I do feel that in so far as the thousands and thousands of young men who to-day serve the navy are concerned, those who are officers but who had not served before the war and who are giving of their best, consideration should be given to enable some of those officers to achieve ranks beyond that which they have been able to secure up to date. I should like to have a statement from the minister of the number of R.C.N.V.R. officers of the rank of commander and senior
thereto; the number of senior officers above the rank of captain who have been retired from the service during the last year; and whether there is in the navy any system similar to that referred to the other day by the Minister of National Defence for Air, under which senior officers are being retired because to retain them in their present positions would mean a ceiling on promotions for other officers lower in rank.
There is just another point, with respect to the post-war navy. Naturally, coming from the prairie provinces, I am very proud of the magnificent record made in the navy by the young men from that part of the country who had no previous experience at sea, and I thank the minister for his kind reference in that connection. What about these young men after the war? In the matter of rehabilitation, what about the opportunity for those who so desire to continue in the naval service? There is a very strong feeling in Canada to-day that after the war Canada should maintain a two-ocean navy. The minister may disagree with that view; but Doctor Weir, director of training in the Department of Pensions and National Health, in presenting a report to the House of Commons reconstruction committee on February 23, said he had questioned many thousands of people across Canada and that the people questioned were in favour of maintaining a two-ocean navy and a modern merchant marine, with permanent navy, army and air force personnel.
The question I ask in that regard is this. Is anything being done to-day to the end that before the war is over there will be a plan in that regard? I do not think that is looldng too far ahead, for concentration now on the matter of rehabilitation will prevent confusion when the war is over. I realize that no permanent plans can be made; wre do not know as yet what will be the course of events. The future must unfold; but the men who serve, the men who have received the technical training to qualify them to fill technical positions in the navy, should be given some hope of securing positions in the navy after the war, and of being rehabilitated in that way. There is not a Canadian who is not proud of what has been done in connection with the expansion of our navy during this war, and of the exploits of our sailors. I wish to say to the minister that any suggestions we make from this side of the house are made in that spirit. I would not want him to take the position he seems to be taking this afternoon, that these suggestions are made in a desire to embarrass him or the navy, or with any improper purpose. When I look back over the past four years and think of the suggestions that have come from this side of the house

War Appropriation-Naval Services
which were frowned upon and criticized when they were advanced, but later accepted, I do not feel it necessary.to apologize on behalf of the opposition for bringing forward constructive ideas and suggestions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Was that the tin-pot navy?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is just what we would expect to hear from Brant county and from the mentality representing it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am not going to answer that remark. If that is the hon. member's contribution to this serious debate I have nothing more to say.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The matter to which the hon. member referred last year, namely, insurance for service men, has been under consideration chiefly, I think, by the pay experts of the services, who have studied the United States system and various alternatives. I must tell my hon. friend frankly .however, that as yet there has been no decision as to what type of insurance, if any, we should adopt. The matter is still in the study stage by the three services combined.
Then the hon. member wanted to know the number of men in the naval volunteer reserve with the rank of commander and higher, and also the number of men of the rank of captain, or higher who were retired in the last year. Probably it will take some hours to secure that information; however, I shall be glad to get it and place it on record for my hon. friend. Then he wanted to know if in the navy there was any policy in regard to retirements similar to that referred to by the minister for air. Beyond the retiring ages fixed by naval regulations-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
What are those
ages?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: They vary according to rank. In the executive branch the age runs from forty-five to sixty-five; in the engineering branch it runs from forty-five to sixty and, in the accounting branch from fifty to sixty, depending on rank. Beyond these age limits we have no arrangement in the navy as to retirement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is the retirement automatic in the various age groups?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Yes.
My hon. friend then spoke of rehabilitation, and I agree with what he said. I think he had in mind particularly a determination now of the size the navy should be after the war, so that those men who might wish to choose the navy as a career could adopt that type of rehabilitation, if I may put it in that way.
The only fixed figure we have as to naval strength shows a total of about 8,700. That was the figure laid down and agreed to by the government in 1941; but, as I pointed out the other day, the staff have prepared various plans showing different strengths for the navy after the war. In most cases the strength suggested exceeds 8,700. It is impossible, I think, to say at this moment exactly what will be the strength of the navy after the war.
I hope it will be reasonably strong, reasonably large in number and reasonably adequate for the purposes the Canadian navy might have to serve, but we have not gone beyond that figure. I think that is the only figure 'that has been laid down by any of the three services; I do not believe the air force or the army have endeavoured as yet to fix definitely what will be their post-war strength.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I should like to pay tribute to the way in which the youth of Canada rallied to the navy at the advent of war. Very often the utterances we hear from the government side of this chamber might lead one to think all this has been done through the navy department itself, but in my opinion that department is being pushed on by the youth of this country who are so anxious to serve in that branch of the service. I congratulate the hon. member for Brandon, who made some observations in regard to graduates of the sea cadet school in that city, many of whom had never seen salt water before joining the navy. I recall that on one occasion I was grounded in Regina when passing through on a plane, and on that Sunday I had the pleasure of seeing in the Presbyterian church across from the hotel an exercise which was being held by four hundred sea cadets of that city. Perhaps ninety-nine per cent of the enthusiastic youth of Canada who enlisted in the navy had never before seen salt water; yet there is something in their make-up which makes them want to serve, and they are doing something really fine for Canada.
I rose particularly to say that we in Toronto have a large enrolment in the naval services. Their exploits and the work they are doing certainly deserves mention in this honourable chamber. Unfortunately in Toronto we do not have a headquarters for naval work. Executives, and those charged with responsibility, find themselves in rented quarters. Some space is given without cost. 1 would ask the minister to see that that important centre in Ontario may have a headquarters for the navy.



War Appropriation-Naval Services
Toronto has given about three and a half acres of land close to the waterfront in the westerly section of the city, near the exhibition grounds. Then, in the eastern portion there is also to be given to the unit looking after sea cadets another strip of ground without cost to the department. That ground, at Kew beach, is bounded on the east side by Kippen-davie avenue and on the west by Kenilworth avenue.
We shall be maintaining naval services after the war, and we should have a headquarters in Toronto. T am hopeful that, as to-day, we may train our boys in the sea cadet movement. At present those boys are being trained in school and church basements, or whatever space can be secured. The supervision they receive is the best, but the facilities for training and the space provided are not at all adequate.
Toronto is peculiarly located. It has some sixteen miles of waterfront, the population being placed east, west, and north, with the lake to the south. It is my opinion that the westerly section of Toronto could be served by a headquarters building, provided that building had one or two decks in which the boys could be trained. The present quarters are located some twelve or fourteen miles away from a large section of the city east of the Don river, where there are some 250,000 inhabitants. People from that area would have to travel the entire width of the city to reach the west end. So that when the vote is before the committee for the headquarters in Toronto, with respect to the three and a half acres in the westerly section, I would ask the department to give consideration to establishing in the easterly section at least one or two decks in which the sea cadets might properly be housed and cared for, so that boys in the eastern part of Toronto might have proper training.
I am hopeful that the minister will make some definite statement this session as to the policy of the department. The matter is now before the city council of Toronto. Within the last two or three weeks representations were made by His Worship the Mayor asking what the attitude of the department was with respect to a headquarters in that city. When they are considering those plans I suggest something must be done for the sea cadets. One or two years after joining the cadet movement those boys find their way to the naval services, and we must do everything we possibly can to help them in that regard.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Thus far I have not taken part in the debate. I am, however, constrained to say something because of the speeches made this afternoon. I was impressed, as I think all hon. members were, with the very fine statement the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services was able to make in respect of the organization of the navy, a*id the good work it is doing. I have spoken to many men who have received technical training with the navy since the beginning of the war, and all have been high in their praise of the quality of that training. The more thoughtful ones, however, were wondering to what use the training could be put when the war is over. Before the war they found themselves in dead-end occupations, and they are wondering if they will have to go back to those occupations or none at the end of the war.
I do not believe the answer to that question can be decided altogether by the size of our navy after the war. If I understood the hon. member for Lake Centre correctly, he said that some people in Canada were talking about a two-ocean navy. He did not explain exactly what a two-ocean navy was, and I do not know what the term means. I believe the size of our navy when the war is over will depend upon the obligations we shall assume in the post-war period for the maintenance of world peace. If any organized attempt is to be made to maintain world peace at the close of the war, as I believe there should be and must be if we are to avoid other wars, then undoubtedly Canada will have to assume her share in that regard. We shall have to be prepared to send armed forces, if necessary, to put down aggression, after a decision has been made that aggression exists. I agree with the minister that that cannot be decided to-day, nor can it be decided until we know what post-war conditions will be.
I hope that we may so arrange our economy in Canada that we can harness the energy of the young men in the various armed services and in industry, and give them social objectives that will be as strong as the national objectives they were given in preparing themselves for war. If we do not do that there is very little hope that they will be any better off after the war, regardless of the size of our navy, than they were before the war when we had practically no navy at all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I was keenly interested in what was said a few moments ago by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I

War Appropricdion-Naval Services
hope, however, that if we ever find ourselves going into another war we shall not be in the same position we were in when we entered this one. In passing, may I say that one of the reasons why we were unprepared for the present war was the attitude of hoa. members in the party to which the hon. member belongs. Pacifist expressions came from them. Every time estimates were before the committee, hon. members in that group were trying to cut them down. It was only because of the real understanding by men in the Royal Canadian Navy at that time that we did have a nucleus which, at the beginning of this war, was able to expand to such a great extent.
The hon. member for Danforth has just referred to establishing a naval headquarters at Toronto. I agree with him, but I think we must go farther than merely having a headquarters at that point. As I have said before in the committee when discussing the estimates, the people of Toronto have always been keen in their interest in the navy. My suggestion is that we should have not only a headquarters, but something better than that. I say that we should have some real, fighting ships. Perhaps they would not be able to carry guns, but we could have those ships, to be used for training the young men who want to enter the navy. In that way we would have preparedness, and the youth of our country would be trained on real ships.
While I do not believe that we have any desire to detract attention from the winning of the war, at the same time some plans must be laid for after the war. Many men who have never been on ships before, will, after the war is over, not want to go back to farming or various other occupations but will prefer to sail on ships. Has any planning been done in connection with our merchant marine? There is no doubt that with its great lakes and two oceans Canada should have a great merchant marine. We should be able to have our ships operating from Canada to all the ports of the globe, thus presenting great opportunities for a livelihood to men who will be coming out of the navy when the war ends. It is not beyond the bounds of possibility that the St. Lawrence great waterway may become an all-winter route to the sea. Certainly it will have access to the sea for longer and longer periods as the years go by. There should be an opportunity for the men who have served in the navy to enter the merchant marine after the war and make it their life work. Can the minister tell us what planning has been done along that line?
The hon. member for Danforth spoke of the naval barracks which are to be constructed in Toronto and made certain suggestions. Would the minister give us a full outline of what is proposed?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish this group had the great influence which the hon. member for St. Paul's implies we have or had. It is amazing how a party of seven members out of the 245 could block necessary military preparations if such preparations were necessary, and I may have something to say about that later. But now may I draw to his attention that the smallest appropriation for military services ever voted by parliament within my memory, was voted when the hon. member's own party was in office between 1930 and 1935. At that time his party were, if I remember correctly-and I have been so told on many occasions by people who ought to know-so intent on building up proper armed services in order that this country could meet the world single-handed, that the men in the militia had even to buy their own shoes and other equipment. It was under the Bennett government also, I believe, that what little air force we had was scrapped. This group was not responsible for that. Other conditions arose between 1930 and 1935, and no action was taken to meet them. There was a very serious unemployment situation in this country. Was it because of opposition from this group that nothing was done for the unemployed? Was it because of opposition from this group that when the war came, many people were in such poor physical condition that they were not fit for military service?

War Appropriation-Naval Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I should like to have an answer to my question about the naval barracks in Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The question would come more properly under another item, but I can answer my hon. friend now. We have decided to build a naval barracks in the city of Toronto, as wag announced last Thursday. I should hope that the sea cadets, as is customary in most places, would have certain facilities in that headquarters. I sympathize with the hon. member for Danforth whose sea cadet corps, I understand, is rather too far away to be able to make full use of the facilities of the new barracks, and he suggested that we might perhaps establish some sort of headquarters on the east side of Toronto. I must tell my hon. friend that we have not in mind at the moment the building of a second barracks or headquarters for the naval service in Toronto. As to the sea cadets we have never endeavoured :n the naval service to build special facilities for them, but we have always been happy to make available to them any buildings and facilities that we had. In some cities, like Montreal for instance, the Navy League raised a certain sum of money and was able to build a most handsome addition to an existing building for their sea cadets. I am sorry to have to tell my hon. friend that as far as the navy is concerned I do not think we could undertake, apart from providing some accommodation in the barracks, to build or otherwise acquire any accommodation for the sea cadets, much as I am interested in the movement and deeply as I appreciate the good work the movement is doing throughout Canada.

Mr. Chairman, with the consent of the committee I

The leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) asked a question with regard to sergeant-pilots on leave without pay at civilian operated schools. His questions and the answers are as follows: Question:
1.	How are sergeant-pilots chosen to be on leave without pay for civil-operated schools?
2.	What is the basis?
3.	How many of them are there?
Answer:
1.	Staff pilots on leave without pay are now employed at air observers schools only. Procedure for choosing staff pilots is as follows:
A request is received from the manager of an air observers school for a certain number of pilots. Instructions are issued by air force headquarters to the commanding officers of secondary flying training schools to select this number of suitably trained graduates. By "suitably trained" is meant trained on twin-engine aircraft and above average in navigation. Personnel so selected by their C.O.'s are posted to the air observers schools on service strength. If they prove satisfactory, and acceptable to the civilian manager, after a reasonable period of service, they are requested to make application through the R.C.A.F. chief supervisory officer at the school and the civilian manager to be released on leave without pay. The application is reviewed at air force headquarters, and if satisfactory, the pilot is struck off strength on leave without pay.
Occasionally, the civilian manager of an air observers school will request the services of a specific pilot who has been employed on staff or instructional duties at an R.C.A.F. training unit, and who has a large number of flying hours to his credit. Each of these cases is reviewed strictly on its merits, with due regard for the individual's value to the R.C.A.F. in that capacity at that particular time.
All pilots on leave without pay at civil-operated schools are subject to immediate recall at any time.
2.	Answered in question 1.
3.	Figures for sergeant-pilots alone are not immediately available. The total number of staff pilots on leave without pay at eight civil-operated air observer schools at 29th February, 1944, was 596. A very few might be officers, the remainder being non-commissioned officers.

The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked a question with regard to annotated positions and the number of officers who thereby secure exemption from income tax. The questions and answers are as follows:
1.	Q. The minister possibly can give us an answer that will cover the situation by telling us the number of administrative officers who fill annotated positions and who thereby secure exemption from income tax although they are not actually engaged in flying.
A. Only general list positions are annotated and in the event of a non-flying list person filling a general list position which is exempt from income tax, the non-flying list person is not exempt from income tax by reason of the position annotation.
2.	Q. And will the minister give the committee a list of the annotated positions?
A. It would take considerable clerical work to complete a list of all annotated positions but it is felt that the following definition of the policy covering position annotations will suffice:
(a)	The following positions are annotated:
(i)	All general list positions established for aircrew duties.
(ii)	The commanding officers of stations where the primary function is flying operations.
(b)	The following positions are NOT annotated:
(i)	Any position at air force headquarters or the headquarters of a command, group or wing.
(ii)	The commanding officers of units whose primary function is not flying, e.g., repair depots, wireless schools, initial training schools, equipment depots, etc.
