Questions were asked by various members with regard to civilian flying schools. The answer is as follows:
Re: Civil Flying Schools E.F.T.S. When it was decided that flying clubs should be asked to sponsor E.F.T.S. pains were taken to appoint a committee consisting of the most competent and experienced people available. This committee included: Colonel K. S. McLaughlin, then Acting Deputy Minister of National Defence; Air Marshal G. M. Croil, then C.A.S.; Brigadier Orde, Judge Advocate General; Mr. M. A. Seymour, K.C. and Mr. C. W. Nicholl, C.A. as representing the Canadian Flying Clubs Association; Mr. Henry Borden, K.C.; Mr. H. G. Norman, C.A., now Financial Adviser to the B.C.A.T.P. This committee drew up a form of contract as between the Crown and the individual operating companies, in most eases sponsored by the flying clubs. It had no experience to draw upon; yet the form of contract has functioned fairly satisfactorily with the exception that the remuneration proved somewhat generous and took the following form:
(a)	Savings on management fee.
(b)	Profit per flying hour.

(c)	Savings on gasoline and oil.
(d)	Savings on crash reserve.
(e)	25 per cent savings on operation and maintenance.
The contract provided for an adjustment between the contractual parties at the end of each 24 weeks period to be based on the experience of the previous 24 weeks.
The schools were originally opened to provide for a pupil population of 48 and all were from time to time increased to a pupil population of 90, 120, 180 or 240.
These increases detracted from the value of the cost of operation experience gained when endeavouring to apply these in adjusting the allowances by the crown.
The various sources of profit or savings which I have mentioned also tended to complicate the situation and this was brought out at the enquiry before the parliamentary committee.
In an endeavour to simplify the situation, the operating companies voluntarily agreed to reduce their flying hour profit from 50 cents to 25 cents and later to eliminate it.
They also agreed to forgo profits or savings on gasoline and oil as well as on their crash reserve. No fees were paid to directors and the only disbursement made out of profit was the 5 per cent dividend on the subscribed capital.
All surplus funds accruing in the hands of the operating companies were invested in noninterest beai'ing certificates of the Dominion of Canada.
When the contracts were renewed as on the 1st April, 1943, the above concessions were legalized, management was included in operation and maintenance and all savings on operation and maintenance were made divisible as to 80 per cent and 20 per cent between the crown and the companies, instead of 75 per cent and 25 per cent as heretofore.
These concessions or modifications have resulted in considerable savings to the crown. At the same time the subscribed capital of these companies was refunded to shareholders out of surplus in the hands of the companies, thus eliminating the dividend.
The companies have now only one source of profit which is the savings on operation and maintenance and the contract declares ". . . that any savings or profits accruing shall not be distributed and shall be held by the company in a reserve account until the termination of the contract and shall then be paid to a flying club approved by the minister, failing which they shall revert to the crown."
During the operation of these contracts, the pro forma or basis for payment to these companies have been carefully revised at the end of each 24 weeks period and despite the revision downwards per pupil population intake, the companies, through increased efficiency in operation, have continued to make savings, some of them more than others, depending upon the efficiency in operation, the terrain in which they function, etc.
The modifications in the terms and conditions of the contract and the concessions demanded from time to time have been immediately and generously conceded by the operating companies who have declared that they are more anxious to do a good job than to make profits. Their only desire is that upon completion of the contract, each school will be able to hand over

War Appropriation-Air Services
to its sponsoring flying club sufficient funds to rehabilitate its club so that it may in the post-war period continue in advancing civil aviation in Canada.
A special form of charter and by-laws under part II of the Dominion Companies Act have been drawn up and approved by my department under which any club benefiting from these profits must be incorporated and w'hich protect such profits in the hands of the flying clubs from being exploited.
A meeting of managers of all E.F.T.S. was held lately when they agreed to recommend to their directors that all and any profits or
savings, accruing from the operation of their school and in turn to their sponsoring flying club, be limited to $5,000 per annum. Resolutions of the board of the various operating companies to this effect are now being received.
Of the 80 per cent savings in operations $1,951,404.40 has actually been returned to the crown and a further $1,250,000 is now available for return, for which demands are being sent out this month, in accordance with the terms of the agreement.
Up to 2nd January last, 38,775 pupils have graduated from E.F.T.S. at an average cost of $911.55 per pupil.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENTS BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM, THE U.S.S.R, AND AUSTRALIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by arrangement with the other governments concerned, I desire to lay on the table at this time, copies of general Mutual Aid agreements which have been concluded between the government of Canada and the governments of the United Kingdom, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics and the Commonwealth of Australia. The agreements with the United Kingdom and Soviet governments were signed on February 11 and the agreement with Australia was signed on March 9. Similar agreements are in process of negotiation with other governments or authorities receiving supplies from Canada in significant volume under the Mutual Aid Act, notably China and the French committee of national liberation.
These agreements set forth the general terms and conditions under which war supplies are being transferred under the Mutual Aid Act to the three countries which have so far received the largest quantity of such supplies from Canada. When the Mutual Aid legislation is before the house there will be an opportunity for discussing the terms of these agreements, if the house so desires. At this time I wish only to give a general explanation of their purpose and contents.
The preamble of the Mutual . Aid Act declares that "it is essential to the defence and security of Canada and to the cause of world freedom that Canada should make the utmost contribution to the victory of the united nations". It continues that "it is necessary that the products of Canadian war industry be made available not only for use by Canadian forces, but also to other united nations, in accordance with strategic needs, in such manner as to contribute most effectively to the winning of the war." The preamble concludes that "it is expedient that the conditions upon which Canadian war supplies are made available to other united nations should
Mutual Aid Agreements

not be such as to burden post-war commerce, or lead to the imposition of trade restrictions, or otherwise prejudice a just and enduring peace". Since early in the war, the government has taken the position that the accumulation of large war debts was contrary to the public interest. This policy has been endorsed by parliament on several occasions. It is to be noted that a similar policy was adopted by the government of the United States with the passage of the Lend-Lease Act on March 11, 1941, nearly nine months before the United States entered the war. The United Kingdom, which is the third large provider of munitions and war supplies for the use of other united nations, has pursued a parallel policy in providing supplies to allied goverments unable to pay for them.
These agreements set forth the general terms and conditions under which effect is being given to our policy. They are in some respects parallel to the Lend-Lease agreements which have been concluded by the government of the United States with many of the goverments receiving supplies from that country under the Lend-Lease Act. It is to be remembered, however, that the Lend-Lease Act was adopted when the United States still retained her neutrality, whereas the Mutual Aid Act was passed when Canada had been at war for over three and a half years. The Lend-Lease Act was based on the conception that the defence of the United States would be furthered by the provision of supplies on other than a cash basis to countries at war with the axis. The Mutual Aid Act was based on a realization that the provision of materials to the common cause was no less vital and no less a duty than the provision of fighting men.
The preamble of these agreements sets forth their purposes in language similar to that used in the preamble of the Mutual Aid Act which I have already quoted. I do not propose to analyse the agreements at any length. They are designed to make clear that the recipient governments accept these purposes and will cooperate in their fulfilment. Article II of each agreement contains a pledge of reciprocal aid to Canada. Article X (article IX in the Soviet agreement) contains a mutual undertaking to pursue international economic policies designed to implement the economic objectives defined in the Atlantic charter and accepted by all the united nations, policies which are reflected in the far-seeing philosophy of the Mutual Aid Act. These policies will make it possible for Mutual Aid
(Mr. Mackenzie King.]
to prove its post-war value in enabling trade to thrive without the barriers which huge war debts would have imposed.
It has been our purpose in instituting the Mutual Aid procedure to leave at the end of the war no indeterminate obligations arising from the provision of war supplies by Canada, which would have to be settled by subsequent negotiations. By article VI of our Mutual Aid agreements it is laid down that the government of Canada will not require the recipient government "to redeliver to the government of Canada any war supplies delivered under this agreement except as specifically provided" in articles VII, VIII, and IX. Article VII provides that title to cargo ships furnished under Mutual Aid shall remain with the government of Canada. Article VIII provides that supplies which, at the end of hostilities in any major theatre, have not yet reached their destination may revert to Canadian ownership. Finally, article IX provides that in certain circumstances the Canadian government may request the transfer of specified types of supplies still serviceable at the end of the war to other users, for relief purposes or for Canadian forces still serving overseas, and that we may also ask for the return to Canada of serviceable aircraft and automotive equipment if required for use at home.
The agreements with the governments of the United Kingdom and Australia are identical in substance. I should explain to the house the reasons for certain minor differences between these two agreements and the agreement with the Soviet government.
Since the German attack on the Soviet Union the war supplies provided to the Soviet government by her allies have been settled by a special procedure which is employed in no other case. Annual protocols have been signed between Russia on the one hand and the supplying countries on the other hand, to which are attached schedules listing the stores which each supplying country undertakes to furnish during the period of one year. The parties of the first two protocols were the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union. Canada is a direct party to the current third protocol which covers the supplies being furnished to Russia during the year which will end on June 30 next. Direct Canadian participation in this third protocol was made possible by the adoption of the Mutual Aid Act at the last session. These protocols are of necessity very secret in character, since they contain information which would be of much value to the enemy.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Article III of the Soviet agreement refers directly to the protocol procedure, and therefore differs somewhat from article III of the other agreements. We have a full opportunity, in the course of the negotiation of the protocol, to secure whatever information is required to support the requests of the Soviet authorities. Article VII in the United Kingdom and Australian agreements is not repeated in the Soviet agreement. It relates specifically to cargo ships, and we have not found it possible to provide the Soviet government with any cargo ships; hence the inclusion of the article in the Soviet agreement is unnecessary. These are the only differences of importance between the agreements.
I now table copies of the agreements.

When we were on the first item the hon. member for Lake Centre raised the question of promotions. I note that at page 1190 of Hansard the Minister of National Defence for Air is reported as having said:
As I said, there is a thick ceiling of comparatively young men at the top. Through no fault of their own, these men have not been able to see active service, and it *was hoped that men who had seen active service would gradually get to the top as they returned from overseas.
And later he said:
I think the country will agree with me in this-because it is imperative that we show these young men that there is a way through this ceiling by which they can get to the top. That is the general policy.
I could not hear what the minister said in reply this afternoon,'but I understood him to say there was no similar policy in his department. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

speechtext:
I do not know that I can add a great deal, except to say that training in the naval service requires a great length of time, I should think probably longer than in either

War Appropriation-Naval Services
of the other two services. That is inevitable, from the nature of the work naval officers have to undertake. They have to be trained not merely theoretically, and on land; there is a certain type of training they can get only at sea, through experience. They have to sail under all sorts of conditions, in all kinds of ships, meeting all kinds of weather, in order to get the training to fit them for their tasks. As I said, we have certain age limits in the naval regulations beyond which an officer cannot go, but other than that we have adopted no policy such as the air force seems to have adopted. I do not think I would want to deviate very much from the policy we have followed in the past. I will say to my hon. friend that from time to time officers are discharged from the naval service. It is an unpleasant duty of mine every week, and sometimes several times a week, to sign memoranda declaring that certain officers are no longer required in the naval service, though usually that is for reasons other than age. As I have said, the age factor is governed by the regulations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What are the present facilities for giving the ratings actual sea training? Have any ships or destroyers been assigned to that work recently, and what has the minister in that line now on the east and west coasts?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend asked that question. For a time we were short in training ships, because every ship that could be put into active service we put on the sea, but now some of the ships are becoming old; some have passed the stage where it pays to repair them, and these are being used as training ships. I do not know the exact number at the moment, though I can get it for my hon. friend; but I know that on the great lakes we have several training ships, not of great .size but nevertheless ships in which men can get considerable training in engine work, helm work and all the other work that goes with the running of a ship. On the east coast we have some ships that are a good deal larger; and as time goes on of course the number of training ships will increase almost automatically, because more and more ships will become worn out and useful only for training purposes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

I doubt if any of the ships on the great lakes were ever ships of war in the true sense, but
I think some of them are as long as 140 feet. They are fairly large, and men can get a good deal of ship experience on them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

To give a direct answer to my hon. friend, however, no policy has been formulated by the government with regard to the creation of a Canadian mercantile marine after the war.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked for the number of naval reserve officers of the rank of commander and above. There are thirty-seven confirmed commanders and above and sixty-three acting commanders and above, or a total of 100 officers of the R.C.N.Y.R. who have obtained the rank of commander and above. The same hon. member asked how many officers of the rank of captain and above have been retired in the past year, including all three branches of the service. As yet none has been actually retired, but two captains of the Royal Canadian Navy are now on leave preparatory to retirement.
The hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) asked me just before six o'clock what the navy had sold by way of salvageable material in the last year. The navy sold in that year salvageable material which realized $60,533.33. This material consisted of scrap metal, clothing, rags, kitchen by-products, equipment, machinery and miscellaneous items, all of which were sold through the acting salvage officer in the Department of Finance.

I have a question to ask, but before doing so I should like to add a brief word to what has been said in praise of the navy. It has been very pleasant listening to the words of hon. members from all sections of Canada, but we from New Brunswick have said nothing. I think that can be attributed to our great modesty. However, it does not mean that we are not proud of the men in the navy who have come from New Brunswick. Possibly we take the sea as a matter of course. A great many of our men earn their living from the sea, not only in time of war, as at present, but in peace time.
We have our full share of men in the navy and more than our share in the merchant marine. We are very proud indeed of the men from our native province who are in both these services. I would say in the words of our great Canadian poet, Bliss Carmen, who was also a New Brunswicker:
Our hearts go sailing outward With the ships of grey Saint John.
My question is in relation to rehabilitation. I believe the hon. member for Souris brought up the matter a few days ago and, in reading Hansard I find that it was discussed under both the army estimates and the estimates for the air force. As a- matter of fact, it was also discussed by the hon. member for St. Paul's. I should like to read what was said with respect to the men who are discharged from the army, and I assume the same applies to the navy at the present time. The hon. member for St. Paul's mentioned some cases in which he thought a rehabilitation allowance

should be given. Replying to the hon. member, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said, as reported at page 622 of Hansard:
My hon. friend will understand that the rehabilitation grant is exactly what it states, namely a grant for the purpose of refitting a man into civilian life.
I do not think anyone can have any argument, as far as that is concerned. Then he goes on to say:
The assumption is that if he takes the option and requests a discharge, he has somewhere to go, some occupation at which he may be engaged. Otherwise he wrould not be asking for the discharge.
My experience has been that all men asking for discharge have not some place to go. There are other reasons for which they ask for discharge. I have found in the army-and I know this must also be the experience in the navy and the air force-that many men ask for discharge on account of sickness in their families. This has often come to my attention as a commanding officer. There are also matters of family trouble, where the head of the family may find that it is better for him to join his family than to stay in the army. Very often the mother in a family is dying, and the father has to go back to look after his children. Then in many cases, too many in fact, it is found that the wife has deserted the children and that someone must look after them. For every case where a . man asks for a discharge to go back to a job I am satisfied there is another case where he asks for a discharge for one of the other reasons I have mentioned. These men are not going back to jobs, and their case is a very difficult one. They are being continually met with.
There is also the question of men who are not fit for overseas service. Hundreds of them 

I think I would be safe in saying thousands of them-are to be found at bases in England, and at depots and other places in Canada, who really have not very much to do in the army. Their position becomes irksome, and they are asking for discharges. But no rehabilitation allowance is provided for them, and they continue in the army.
I believe if some agreement were made, or some programme arranged among the three departments for the release of these men from service, there w'ould be a very large sum of money saved to the country, and justice would be done to the men. Many men are suffering injustices at the present time, because they are simply being told, " You have asked to leave the army. You must have a job to go back to." Accordingly, out they go, without

War Appropriation-Naval Services
any allowance of any kind. I hope that there may be some programmes to look after these men.
As I said a moment ago, anyone who has had anything to do with the administrative work of the different units, in all branches of the services, will come across cases of this kind almost daily. Many of these men who are in the different depots and other base units become tired of the work in the army, and if they go back to their homes they find, if they have been business men, that it takes them some time to get back on their feet. They may have been carpenters, painters, plumbers, or men in other trades. They have been away from their work for three or four years. They may have to buy tools and equipment, so that they can get back on their feet.
Is there- any joint programme either arranged at the present time, or anticipated, to look after the rehabilitation of these men who, I claim, should receive justice. I refer to those who are leaving the army, and many others who should be out of the army at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As I intimated before, and as I believe has been intimated by my colleague, there is a directorate of demobilization in the naval services, and in the other two service departments. There is a combined committee for the three services, a joint'service committee, and also an interdepartmental committee on which I believe my colleagues the Minister of Pensions and National Health and the Minister of Labour are represented as well. They are now giving a great deal of study to this matter of demobilization. I would point out to my hon. friend that once a man is demobilized the responsibility of the three armed services ceases and he becomes the care of the Department of Pensions and National Health. I think my hon. friend was referring at one stage of his remarks to the problem of a man who wants to get out before the end of the wTar, and he asked what is being done for him. Am I correct?
Yes, that is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
With regard to the gratuity, or muste.ring-out pay, or whatever you wish to call it, which he might receive, that matter is at this very moment, and has been, I think, for some two or three months, under consideration by the three service departments and the Department of Pensions and National Health. I am not in a position to say definitely, because I do not think the matter is quite in definite shape, what the financial provisions will be. I think
it is only fair to say that they will be at least as generous as, and I think in most cases more generous than, they were at the conclusion of the last war. My hon. friend from his experience with the army is no doubt familiar with the blue booklet which was sent out showing the possihle training benefits, vocational education and so on that a man may receive who is discharged from the services. These provisions are, I believe, quite generous. In the matter of the young man who left college and wishes to complete his education, there are very generous provisions. In the case of the man who wants to take up farming, very generous assistance is given. I believe that it covers commercial fishing as well. But my hon. friend, having come direct from association with service men, is probably more familiar with that than I am.

I understand the cases which the minister has mentioned. But W'hat I am concerned about is the case of the man who, on account of family trouble or for compassionate reasons, is discharged from the army; his wife has died and he has to look after his children, or the children have been deserted, or there is other serious trouble at home. There are quite a number of these cases. According to the minister, or according to the Minister of National Defence, it is assumed that because a man has asked for his discharge he is going back to his job. The point is that he is not going back to his job, and at the present time no provision is made for these cases, of which a great many are coming up continually. I think the Minister of Pensions and National Health will agree with me that that is the situation, and I think something should be done at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
In
many cases, I assume, the man to whom my hon. friend refers would go back to his job.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: If I may be permitted to intervene, it is at the present time the definite responsibility of the department over which I preside to enable such men to find adequate employment.

Yes, but the fact that it may be the department's responsibility does not mean that the men have the jobs. There

War Appropriation-Naval Services
should be some provision for them until they do get jobs. That is the principle of rehabilitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We have that now.
Well, what about these cases which I have mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We have out-of-work benefits payable for twelve months after discharge if the man is unable to find adequate employment, as well as preferences both in contracts and in government service.
How it works now is that a man is kept on the depot for thirty days and given thirty days pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Of course, if there is any gap at all between his being struck off National Defence and taken up by Pensions and National Health, that gap will have to be closed. I agree, too, that it is our responsibility to apprise the man in the first instance of what he is entitled to in post-war discharge benefits, and, second, to provide him with employment.

The whole point is this. I know the Minister of Pensions and National Health and the other ministers are discussing rehabilitation programmes, and we hear it rumoured that the men will get two or three months pay, or whatever it is. But here are men who have been in the army for three or three and a half years and who go out before the war is over. These men get nothing. I claim that there should be some plan for rehabilitating these men.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: There is. We have found employment for over 85,000.

Further with regard to this matter of the programme, we find a definite reduction in the air force training service programme. I believe the minister for air announced that about twenty-eight flying schools across Canada were being disbanded this year. How will the general programme of naval expansion for 1944 compare with the 1943 programme? Is there any reduction at all?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend means, the number of men to be taken into the service? I would say to him that there will not be as many men taken in during the coming year as there were last year, so that there is a reduction in that regard. On the other hand, the number of ships next year will be greater than it was in the previous year, so that there is an increase there.

Just in connection
with the matter which has been brought up by the hon. member for Royal, the Minister of Pensions andi National Health stated that some 85,000 men had been found employment. If my memory serves me right, some 118,000 have been discharged. Does the minister suggest that all of the 118,000 are in employment and have had no difficulty in securing work?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
No; that is not correct. But I do suggest that, through the direct agency of our organization in the Department of Pensions and National Health, combined with the work of national selective service in the Department of Labour, over 85,000 have been placed. In the last month

I am- speaking from memory now; my hon. friend will pardon me if my figures are not strictly correct-about 3,000 were discharged and placements were found1 for five or six thousand. Of course it is a rotating figure; it is not a fixed figure at all. But we find out that those asking for unemployment benefits are very few, because of the condition of employment in Canada to-day. That condition will not necessarily prevail after the war. I believe there are about three hundred accepting unemployment benefits; that is, those who are waiting for definite employment and who are entitled to the unemployment benefits provided under order in council P.C. 7633.

I assume this would be the right point in the discussion to suggest an amendment of the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act. It is a matter which I think I should bring to the attention of the minister, because no opportunity will be given later on to do so. In 1942 this house passed the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act which as hon. members know, provides that an employer shall reinstate his employee upon discharge from the armed services in the position which he had prior to his enlistment. But there is a provision therein which, I think, is even now being taken advantage of.
Section 4, paragraph (d) provides:
In any proceedings for the violation of section three of this act-
Section 3 sets out what the duty of the employer is with respect to reinstatement.
-it shall be a defence for the employer to prove-
(d) that he-
The discharged soldier.
-was physically or mentally incapable of performing work available in the employer's service.
That section, as things now stand may or may not be taken advantage of. But when

War Appropriation-Naval Services
the war is over and the patriotic urge recedes, and there is a desire on the part of some employers to secure the largest return they possibly can, that section might very well afford a defence to a refusal or a denial of an opportunity for employment to the man who, after service, has been physically disabled in any particular. I raised this point, if I remember correctly, when the bill was up. In the United Kingdom a reinstatement act is in effect, or at all events it was recently introduced, very much along the lines of the act in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: (Vancouver Centre): If my hon. friend will allow me, I do not think the act has been passed as yet in Great Britain, but the bill is very much more comprehensive than the act we passed in Canada two years ago. Our act is confined to ex-service men, while the bill in Great Britain includes those who have been injured in civil accidents, and that is the great criticism against the bill in Great Britain. They say that a man who has served his country in battle should have the preference in reinstatement over a man who has been injured in civil or industrial life. That provision has caused bitter controversy over there.

I am not dealing with the provisions with respect to employers in civilian industry but with the provisions in connection with the reinstatement of men after their discharge from the army. They have found it necessary in Great Britain to pass another act or submit another bill-I do not know whether it is yet law-known as the Disabled Persons bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is the bill to which I was referring.

It is based on the principle that disability is a handicap but not a barrier to employment, and it imposes the obligation upon employers of twenty-five workers or more to take a quota of men and women who are disabled, the quota varying' with the different trades. Has consideration been given in Canada to a similar provision to apply to men who, after service in the armed forces, are discharged by reason of disablement? Is it in the contemplation of the government to introduce some such measure to assure reinstatement for those who, while not physically perfect, are not so handicapped that they could not take employment?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I am afraid I am speaking out of turn more or less by intruding on the estimates of my colleague. The bill passed in Canada a few years ago was sponsored by my colleague the Minister of Labour, although I gave it all
the support I could. The Disabled Persons bill in Great Britain affects civilians as well as ex-service men.
I was referring to ex-service men.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The committees here have been and are considering that very point very carefully. There is no phase of rehabilitation to which keen-minded civil servants in my department and others are not giving serious attention. We are all anxious to do everything we possibly can to meet the very problems my hon. friend has mentioned.
Has consideration been given to that very point?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes, I remember that it was discussed a year ago.

The answer that was given to me by the minister for naval services is the same answer that I have had given to me in half a dozen cases of men who have been discharged on compassionate grounds, not because they wanted to get out of the army or the navy, but for family reasons. I know one of these men in particular whose family has suffered to a great extent. I do not see any reason in the world why men discharged on compassionate grounds cannot be treated exactly the same as men discharged for some other reason. A man who is discharged on compassionate grounds is discharged for a definite reason which is accepted by the department; otherwise he would not be discharged. But he does not get the same discharge pay and allowances as men discharged for other reasons. I have three cases in mind now. In one there was definite hardship. The man had a family of five children and no place to go. The minister of pensions said that these men were all taken care of, but this man was not taken care of. He had great difficulty in getting a job. All he got upon discharge was S35-nothing else-and he has a family of five children. It seems to me that there should not be that discrimination. I think the hon. member for Royal was talking about the same thing that I am talking about now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is something in what my hon. friend says. The man who is discharged because of a death in the family which necessitates his presence at home to look after his family is hardly discharged at his own request. That is one of the points which are now under discussion, together with the whole question of gratuities upon discharge. There is one other point I wish to bring up. We had a long discussion the other night on dependents' allowance in the case of a man who goes A.W.O.L. Would the minister say something about this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

She is in this position-and this particular case is illustrative of many others. The man is in the clink all the time and therefore she gets nothing. She has not heard from him for two years. Surely there must be some remedy. The woman has suffered; what is to be done about it?

There is one other question. In so far as the opportunity now affords itself for men in the lower decks to train for commissions a notable step has been taken. A moment ago the minister, if I understood him aright, stated that there were still exceptions to that rule. What are the exceptions?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There are certain branches of the service into which men come directly. Take as an example the medical branch, the special branch, as it is called, which consists of lawyers, technicians and other professional men. Some men come directly into that branch. But for the executive branch, which is sea-going, what I might call the combatant branch, all entry is made from the lower deck, and I think more than two thousand men have come from the lower deck to commissioned ranks.

Would the minister
give some explanation of the wide variation in the ratio of officers to ratings in the different provinces. The table which was placed on Hansard at page 1309 indicates that Prince Edward Island has a ratio of approximately

four officers to every 100 ratings; Nova Scotia, about ten; New Brunswick, seven; Quebec, thirteen; Ontario, seven; Manitoba, four; Saskatchewan, three; Alberta, three; and British Columbia, twelve. Those of us who come from the prairie provinces will never admit that those who joined the navy from the prairies are not giving a good account of themselves. There are many cases of heroism, and it seemed to me that the ratio from the prairies should be higher. It is hard to understand why the ratio from Prince Edward Island is four compared with ten in Nova Scotia; why the ratio from British Columbia should be so high. It is true that those who live near the sea have opportunities which the prairie boys do not have. In every field of war activity the men from the plains have adapted themselves very quickly to their due responsibilities, and the officers who have been trained have done exceptionally good work. Can the minister explain why there is that variation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is quite natural for my hon. friend to raise the question, and I am glad that he did so because he allows me to make an explanation which perhaps I should have made earlier. It is quite true, as he says, that the proportion of officers to ratings in the prairie provinces is not so high as it is, say in the maritime provinces, or in British Columbia; but I think the reason for that is to be found in the fact that a great many of the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve officers, the men who, before the war, were at sea in the mercantile marine and so on, came from the maritime provinces, the St. Lawrence, the great lakes and British Columbia. I should suppose that very few of the R.C.N.R. officers would come from the prairies because, through the accident of geography, there are no great waterways in those provinces as there are in the five eastern provinces and in British Columbia. Then again there are a great many yachtsmen in the maritime provinces, on the banks of the St. Lawrence, on the great lakes and in British Columbia. These men were available at the beginning of the war and many of them entered the service. On account of their experience with boats and engines and with sail they came into the service. But I should not want it thought for a moment that men from the prairies, given the same amount of training, would not make officers just as competent and just as reliable and faithful in every way as men from any other part of the country. I am sure that they would; they would main-

tain the magnificent record which the prairie provinces have already achieved in the naval service.

The Minister of National Defence put a table on Hansard, which appears at page 990. This table shows that an ordinary seaman signing on gets $1.25 a day; whereas a private in the army gets S1.30. Why the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Well, it is a long story. The fact is that there is some discrepancy all through the table between comparable ranks in the three services. My hon. friend will find, for instance, that certain ranks in the naval service get a little more than the corresponding rank in the army. We find that other ranks get a little less. In the case of the ordinary seaman there was a time when he got $1.45 in the navy, as against the private's S1.30. Then we had to adjust it in some way and we also had to adjust the matter of subsistence. Then, the marriage allowance in the navy was a little bit lower than in the army for some curious reason, and by trying to adjust those things as equitably as we could it was felt that the ordinary seaman who joined the navy after June, 1942, I think it was, should receive $1.25 a day instead of SI.30 for the private. I will agree with my hon. friend that it is difficult to take these tables and find them wholly and absolutely comparable. They are not, but it was about the best we could do at the time.

The [DOT]eason why I brought this matter up was that these boys, when they join the navy, the army or the air force at $1.30 a day, would like to have,a few dollars to spend. But they find they have practically nothing on account of the things they have to buy. I think when they join up they should have the same pay all the way through the services. After they step up it might be a little different, but when they join I really believe they should have the same all the way through.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes. I shall bear that in mind. Certainly I have no objection whatever to seeing their pay raised by five cents.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to deal with a matter relating to transportation home for men who leave the navy, technically at their own request. As the minister knows, I wrote him about a particular case some time ago, and at that time he quoted to me a particular regulation and said it was impossible to do anything in connection with the rating about whom I wrote. Latei*on, thinking the regulation stood for all three services, I raised the matter in the house; I believe it was on February 17, when the Minister of National Defence was before the committee. At that time I learned that a change had been made, with respect to the army at any rate, providing for transportation from the place of discharge, even when a man was discharged at his own request, back to the place of enlistment or to the home of the individual. There was a little confusion that night as to whether the regulations were the same in all three services, but the next day the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services tabled a regulation which had been passed some days earlier, providing for the very thing I was mentioning, namely transportation from the place of discharge to the place of enlistment or the rating's home.
On the basis of that new regulation, even though I knew it was dated in February while the case with which I was dealing went back to December of last year, I drew this case to the attention of the minister again. I did so because I felt that it was a particularly unfortunate case in itself, and also because I felt that there must be other similar cases. This rating had enlisted at London, Ontario. On account of his wife's illness, which was quite serious, it became unquestionably necessary for him to leave the service. I am bearing in mind what the minister said a few moments ago, that there are cases like this in which,

though technically a man is discharged at his own request, still the situation is not of his own creation, and in my opinion special consideration should be given a man under such circumstances. This particular man, who was discharged in Victoria, was given the balance of pay that was coming to him up to that time and the clothing allowance, which at that time was $35. He was told, though he did not need to be told, that he would have to spend that $35 on clothes, which left him with only about $20 or $22 to go from Victoria to near London, Ontario. Eventually the man made contact with the Navy League of Canada in Victoria; and a man whom I happen to know, a former solicitor of the city of Winnipeg working with the Navy League in Victoria, did his best to help this man. When I discussed the case previously I implied that the Navy League of Canada had supplied the money to enable this man to get home. Really that was not the whole of the story. It was through the Navy League and the assistance of the gentleman to whom I have referred that help was obtained for this man. But actually it had to be obtained in the form of borrowed money. The money was lent to him, through the instrumentality of the gentleman to whom I have referred, by the Salvation Army. That was the source to which this man had to go to get money to go home. He is now home. In the meantime he has secured employment again, but he has been faced with very heavy medical bills because of the serious illness of his wife, and he still owes as a debt the money that was borrowed from the Salvation Army to enable him to get home.
As I say, fully conscious of the fact that I was asking for something that dated back prior to the date of the new regulations, nevertheless I felt it was a case that should be given more generous and sympathetic consideration by the minister. Accordingly I wrote him again on March 2, and in his reply to me the minister said he did not think it would be wise to pay transportation in this case, because that would be establishing a precedent. As a matter of fact, I do not think that is any argument against it. If there are cases similar to this, of men who have offered their services, and spent time in the forces, but who through no fault of their own have been forced to get out, and have been left with a debt such as this so that they could get home, it would not do any harm to establish a precedent to treat generously men who find themselves in that situation.
I was a little put out by the comment of the minister when he said at a later point

War Appropriation*-Naval Services
in his letter that he did not altogether approve the paying of transportation in such cases. The minister used these words:
When men are discharged at the end of hostilities, or through wounds, or for other causes not of their own making, then I feel it is only fair for the government to pay transportation.
With that we all agree. But then he goes on to say:
On the other hand, when a man leaves the service for his own private reasons, it seems to me that he is in a totally different position.
I do not think that comment should have been made about a man who has offered his services, spent four years in the navy, and who would have preferred to stay in the navy but who, for reasons not of his creation, because of difficulties at home, is forced to leave the service.
I should like to quote from one letter I received from this man, just to indicate his spirit in the whole matter. As hon. members will realize, after the conversation I had with the Minister of National Defence in this matter in the committee, following which the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services tabled the revised regulations, I conveyed that information to this man. This was his reply to me:
I feel much better now. At least the next fellow that has to be discharged under the same circumstances will fare a whole lot better than I. There is a saying in the navy, "Grim, isn't it?" And that just about sums it all up.
I emphasize the fact that the spirit of this man, despite his unfortunate and unhappy situation, is indeed commendable. I present the case because I feel that in this and similar cases a point should certainly be stretched in their favour.
It has now been recognized under the new regulations in all three services that when a man is discharged at his own request, particularly in a situation such as this, his transportation is paid back to the place of his enlistment, or to his home. That is now the rule in all three services. I make a plea again for this man, and for. other men in similar situations, even though their cases may have been prior to date of the new regulations, and I ask that the department see what can be done by way of taking care of any debt they may have had to incur to get home.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I would have to look up the correspondence. I do not know whether it appeared to me at first that this man was in the position described by my hon. friend. But I still say, generally, that the man who leaves the service at his own request because he thinks he can better 100-98
himself, or for some other such reason, should not be paid by the service for his transportation-although we are doing it, even in that case. The case of the man discharged at his own request under circumstances such as my hon. friend has described, through the illness of some relative or for some other domestic cause which urgently requires his presence at home, is a little different.
When I said I was opposed to paying transportation to a man who left the service at his own request I meant this. Why should the service take any more interest in the man who leaves, as I say, because he wants to go back to farming, into business or something of that sort and hopes to better himself? There is no reason why it should. He leaves when it suits him. We shake hands and part, and that is the end of the transaction.
But in the case my hon. friend describes, one where there was some domestic trouble or domestic worry which compelled him to go home, I agree there is a little difference. However, I am not sure that that was made clear to me in the correspondence. I shall look into it and find out.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I wish to make a plea to the minister in dealing with a case of this kind not to use language such as he did, when he spoke of men leaving the service to better their own positions. I appreciate the minister's offer to look up the correspondence again. He will find I have written him two letters, each of which was two pages in length, in which I gave far more detail than I have given on the floor of the house. The details make it clear that it was a case in which generous treatment should have been given the man. It was in no sense any attempt to better his position, but simply because there were reasons why he had to go home.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
My hon. friend may have written me two letters, but I get a great many letters, and I cannot attempt to recall what was in a letter written to me a .month or six weeks ago. I am sorry, but that is the situation. I should like to have time to look up the correspondence, and see whether it was made abundantly clear that it was not so much a case of a man's being discharged at his own request as one where the circumstances imperatively required his presence at home. I have every sympathy with such a case.
I have not so much sympathy, however, with the man who, to better his own position, says, "I want to go farming. I have had a year or two in the navy, and I want to leave it." He should pay his own way home. But



War Appropriation-Naval Services
even in that case, under the recent ruling, we pay his way. But I draw a distinction between the purposes for which a man wants to leave the service. If it is for a commendable purpose, for what might be called humanitarian reasons, that is one thing. I have every sympathy with that. But if it is because a man wishes to go home only because he thinks he can make more money, then I say that is his own lookout, and he should pay his own way.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I object, and the reason why I have protested so vigorously against the minister making the comments he has made in this case is that, in spite of the detail which I have placed before him-and I think, when he examines the correspondence in the light of this discussion, he will see my point-the direct statement he made was, "I do not think it would be wise to pay transportation in this case."
I shall draw the case to the minister's attention again by correspondence, and I am sure after what has been said to-night he will look into it further.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall be glad to look into it further.

On an earlier occasion, when the estimates of the Minister of National Defence were before the committee, a number of hon. .members made a further plea for free transportation for members of all services when on furlough or on embarkation leave. We were told then that the matter was under consideration. Has any decision been arrived at up to this time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The matter of free transportation for members of the armed services has been brought up in the house almost every session in the last three or four years. I do not know that we can ever go so far as to give free transportation to members of the armed services to all parts of Canada, but there has been a suggestion-that is all I can say; it is now under consideration -that we fix a certain maximum payment beyond which the soldier, the sailor or the airman would not have to go. That, I may say, is quite a reasonable maximum, and it may be agreed to. But it would be difficult to grant free transportation all round in a country as great as Canada. I recognize that in the United Kingdom service men are given free transportation, but there the distances are much shorter than they are from one side of Canada to the other, and the matter is a good deal simpler.

I think one of the main reasons why this question has been brought up so

often is the size of our country. In a number of cases men who belong in Vancouver are stationed on the east coast, and it costs them quite a lot of money to get to the west coast. So that if a ceiling is determined upon, I hope it will be set very low.

speechtext: If my hon. friend would send me over the name by secret message I could look it up here.

Then we would not have the privilege of getting on Hansard the location of a most elaborate and up-to-date building. It is at Matsqui, in the Fraser Valley. I understand there is no "hush, hush" about it. It is an interceptor station.

cannot tell my hon. friend exactly what it is proposed to do there, but I may say that a considerable sum is set aside in the estimates for construction of works and buildings at three places out there, of which I assume Aldergrove is one. should like to ask the minister how much more it will cost to complete Deep Brook, or Cornwallis, and, if possible, I should like to know how much it has cost so far.

At

That
is why I wondered if the minister was going to extend the wharf out.

Could the
minister state what the depth of water is at that dock at average high tide and the depth of water at extreme low tide?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

I see that this item covers buildings only and that the sum of 817,990,462 covers expenditures in connection with the erection of other new buildings or repairs to old buildings. Would the minister give a break-down of that amount, showing what will be spent on new buildings and what will be spent on old buildings; also a breakdown of the 86,715,891 into the three separate items of repairs, operating expenses and rentals.

Did I understand the minister to say that at high tide the depth of water at the wharf at Deep Brook was twenty feet, and that there was no depth of water at low tide?

It is supposed to be a fairly good building?

Have any new properties been acquired for the sea cadets?
Mr. MACDONALD'(Kingston City): As I intimated to the hon. member for Danforth this afternoon, we do not pay for any of these sea cadet camps. There were no new camps taken over in the past year?

That is the question I asked: not the cost, but which new ones were acquired.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

None of them belonging to the dominion government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.

Last year the sea cadet camp on the west coast was at Comox, and I was informed it was not the intention of the minister to use it again for that purpose. Does the minister know whether that is the case?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I cannot answer my hon. friend. Is the camp being put to some other purpose this year; is that the question?
What I was told was that another site more suitable for the purpose of a sea cadet camp was being considered and that it -was not likely that Comox would be used again.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

During the past year have any new barracks been built for the Wrens, or are any new ones contemplated this year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Speaking subject to possible correction, I think the only new building we actually erected for the Wrens was at St. John's, Newfoundland. We did acquire several existing buildings in several parts of the country for the use of the Wrens, and in fact we built other buildings, too.

They are under rental?

This afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver South spoke at some length on the war against Japan in the Pacific. While I, too, am a Vancouver member, I must say that I am more in accord with the views of the minister and the hon. member for Broadview in that our job with the navy is the battle in the north Atlantic. We in British Columbia are aware of the fact that the Canadian navy will eventually fight in the Pacific against the Japanese. Having that in mind, may I ask how much of the $17,000,000 to be spent in the current year will be spent in the great harbour of Vancouver, where certainly the British navy and parts of the Canadian navy will be based at dockyards and piers, which will have to be built in advance, without detracting from the efficiency of Canadian ships in the north Atlantic.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The question of works and projects to be undertaken in Vancouver harbour is still under consideration. There is ample scope within the estimates to take care of any expenditure which we may find it necessary to make there, but the whole discussion is still proceeding and nothing definite has been settled as to just what will be done in the harbour.
Is this discussion based on the needs of Canada's navy out there at the present time or on the basis of what the British navy and the Canadian navy will need when they fight Japan?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend will allow me to give a little thought to that question and bring down the answer later. We did acquire from the Department of Transport the right to use certain sheds on one of the harbour commission piers in Vancouver and that helped us out for the time being. I am not sure, and I do not think anyone in the department is sure, whether that will be sufficient to take care of our needs. It may be that we shall have to put up still more storage space in Vancouver harbour, but that is a matter which is still being considered and which I should like to have an opportunity of thinking over before replying.

I think the war in the Pacific will involve more than a few sheds and a government pier. I suggested the other evening that the great harbour space in North
Vancouver could be used. It is not a matter of building docks when the war actually develops out there.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is not a matter of building docks now? I thought my hon. friend was advocating the building of a naval dock.
I am advocating just that, on the north shore of Vancouver harbour.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
thought my hon. friend said it was not a matter of building docks. I did not hear him correctly. I shall be glad to give him a considered answer later. I have no doubt he is interested in the harbour of Esquimalt. There is an estimate for Esquimalt of $968,000 in connection with the dockyard joint service magazine and fueling depot at that point. If my hon. friend will be good enough to let me look at the Vancouver matter I shall give him an answer later.
Will the minister look up for me the aggregate item? I am interested in knowing whether there is provision there for the locality with which I am concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I told my hon. friend there was an aggregate item of $187,000, and I am sure his locality is one of the places to be taken care of under that item.
I am afraid the $187,000 represents money spent last year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Oh, no. This is for the next year.

May I refer to the question of camps for sea cadets. Did I understand the minister to say that such a camp was located at Wabamun, near the city of Edmonton? Would the minister tell the committee the size of the camp, when it was located there, and whether there are any other camps in Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The Wabamun camp was under the supervision of Edmonton. There was another camp, the Chestermere lake camp, fourteen miles from Calgary. These are the only two in Alberta. The number of boys attending Wabamun camp was 119, and those attending Chester-mere lake camp, 462.
If the minister would be considerate enough to lower his voice we might hear what is being said behind the curtains.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend.

May I ask a question with regard to the gymnasium at Wellington barracks? The cost of this gymnasium would appear to the ordinary person to be extravagant, most excessive. I do not want to be interpreted as criticizing expenditures for giving all the equipment, facilities and comfort necessary to the men in the navy. I think it is the view of the people of Canada that there is nothing too good for the navy. They have the good will of everybody, particularly the women all over Canada. On the other hand, when there is an expenditure of 8645,000 or thereabouts for a gymnasium and swimming-pool in connection with Wellington barracks a great many people in my province wonder if this very large expenditure is really necessary. Many people who subscribe according to their means to bonds and pay heavy taxes have serious misgivings about some of those excessive expenditures or what they interpret as excessive expenditures in connection with the minister's department. The department has expanded greatly since the outbreak of the war. At that time it had only 1,774 men in the service, and the whole Canadian navy, big and small, was represented by fifteen vessels. I do not hold the minister to account for that. But I say the figures which were given as the basis of the growth of the navy are a most serious reflection on the government and those who had the responsibility of preparing Canada to defend itself and its shipping when war broke out. The minister was not in his present position at that time, and I do not hold him responsible. On the other hand, I consider it to the discredit of those who had the responsibility in the years leading up to the war.	[DOT]
I should like to ask the minister what is the justification for this veiy large expenditure on the gymnasium built at Wellington barracks, Halifax, which I think has the special name of Stadacona?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
can only say to my hon. friend that it is a very large physical training building. The estimate is considerably less now than the original estimate. The original estimate was cut down quite drastically. There is a swimming-pool in the building, but I think that is an absolute necessity for men who are taking on duties at sea; and to show that there is no extravagance I received not long since a letter from a citizen of Halifax who urged that the swimming-pool should be, as most swimming-pools are, tiled instead of lined with cement. He pointed out that tile was much more sanitary, that men were likely to contract athlete's foot one from another if cement were used. We
fMr. A. L. Macdonald.]
have not agreed even to spend the extra five or six thousand dollars that it would cost to t.ile that swimming-pool and the adjacent floor.
This is a physical training building. It is very large. It is well fitted out but not extravagantly fitted out. I can get my hon. friend more details by to-morrow; but I think I can assure him that every economy which could be reasonably practised was practised there.

This expenditure may be justified, but a great many of the taxpayers do not appreciate that it is. That expenditure would build practically the entire equipment of some of the smaller universities that we have down east. What composes the whole set-up of Wellington barracks? I understand that one part of it is called Stadacona No. 1 and another part Stadacona No. 2, and perhaps there are other sections of the naval establishment at Wellington barracks. Could the minister give the committee this information ?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Stadacona No. 2 is what used to be called the "Y" depot, the building used by the air force. Stadacona proper, that is, the old Stadacona, is the original site. My hon. friend is familiar with it. I may say with regard to the physical training building that a great many men would rely on this physical training building for physical training and exercise. For instance, at Stadacona there are roughly 12,000 men. That does not take in men who might be visiting the port in ships.
They are all allowed to go into the swimming-pool?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Oh,
yes, it is for all naval personnel. They are allowed not merely to go into the swimming-pool but to use the parallel bars and all the physical training appliances in this building. No university in this country has anything like 12,000 men or men and women put together. No university here has half that number, so that there is, I think, a great need for a proper physical training building.
May I suggest to the minister that if there is any question about giving them tile, give them the tile.

I should like
to ask the minister what interest his department has in connection with the old exhibition grounds and the exhibition equipment at Halifax? I am not sure whether it is under the control of the army or the navy. I understand that the navy has an interest in part of it at least. This property was taken over from the province of Nova Scotia, as I understand it, for

War Appropriation-Naval Services
the sum of $225,000, or thereabouts. I am not sure whether that includes the entire property. Large expenditures were made on it, the contractors being the Fundy Construction company, S262,606; R. & A. Parsons, $323,293; W. G. Foley, $59,778, and nearly $70,000 in furnishings and equipment. Then there are the grandstand and the outer building. I should like to know what part of this building is used by the Department of National Defence for Naval Services and whether the minister's department is responsible for this additional building or works constructed on the property?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
think I can say to my hon. friend that the army now has control of all the exhibition building and grounds. We were there for a time, and we may now have a small storehouse on one corner of it for the storage of minesweeping gear, but I think the army is exclusively in control there.
Were these new structures built by the army or by the minister's department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not think we built any new structures, certainly no large ones. We had to do some building there because men were sleeping under the grandstand for a time. We had to put in bunks and we had to put in heating and so on. Inevitably what would be suitable as an exhibition building would not be suitable as a barracks, and therefore we had some repair work to do on the building. Now the whole matter is under the army.

I understand the King Edward hotel has been purchased by the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. For what purpose is it being used, and was due consideration given by the department to the inconvenience of the other users of this property when they were displaced, in view of the great scarcity of hotel accommodation in the city of Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: At the moment I cannot give my hon. friend the cost to us of the King Edward hotel, but my recollection is that this building had not been used as a hotel for a great number of years. We took over the King Edward hotel and certain other adjacent property, and are using it now as a canteen, cafeteria, restaurant and that sort of thing.
I see by a return which was brought down that the property was purchased for $26,500.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It was a very good buy.

Then I should like to ask the minister about the construction of the wireless and telegraph station at Dartmouth. A fairly considerable expenditure has been made there to the Fundy Construction company, amounting to $129,751. What is that used for?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I presume my hon. friend refers to Albro lake, outside Dartmouth. If my hon. friend wishes to know the total cost I shall have to get that information for him, but the work there is for a wireless station.
Then I should like to ask with regard to the very large expenditure on the navy armament depot at Dartmouth, which appears to have cost nearly $3,000,000. For what purpose is that required?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That will be for the storage and repair of guns of all kinds.
If repairs are carried on there, is it equipped with a machine-shop capable of doing general overhaul work?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes; storage and repair.

What is the policy of the department with respect to /the searching of titles and other legal services? Mr. J. E. Rutledge has many accounts in, though in connection with some of them his charges are not known. I see the name of Mr. J. W. Godfrey, and there are several others. Have Mr. R. M. Fielding, Mr. J. W. Godfrey and Mr. COMMONS

Naval Services
J. E. Rutledge any special qualifications beyond those possessed by scores of other solicitors in the city of Halifax for doing this work for the department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I told my hon. friend a moment ago that I do not appoint any of these men. These matters are handed to the Department of Justice, which selects the men who are to act for it in the various localities. As to Mr. Rutledge, Mr. Godfrey and Mr. Fielding, I think any of them would be quite competent to search titles.

Then I should like to get some information with respect to the naval set-up at Point Edward, I think, in Westmount, at Sydney harbour on Cape Breton island. What has been the total expenditure there; what is the equipment, and for what purpose is it used? While the minister is dealing with this, I should like to know the loss that was entailed in the fire which occurred a few months ago and whether he has any information as to the cause of the fire at that establishment, as well as the causes of fires at various other defence establishments not only in Nova Scotia but elsewhere throughout Canada. A great deal of uneasiness has been caused among people generally by these fires which have destroyed establishments either under the control of the department or erected for the convenience and comfort of men in the services. Great losses have been caused to those who for patriotic reasons have made personal contributions in order to see that the enlisted men should have all possible advantages and comforts.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The amount expended at Sydney to December 31 last was $9,662,000, and it is estimated that it will cost $840,000 to complete the work. My hon. friend asked as to the purpose of this institution. There is at Sydney a complete naval base consisting of barracks, officers' quarters, canteens, mess halls, wardrooms, schools, training accommodation, store buildings, recreation facilities, shops, laundry, bakery, post office, a marine railway, fire station, pump station, chapel, hospital and so on. It is a fairly complete naval base.
Would the minister give information as to the cause of the fire at Point Edward or Westmount, and other points in Nova Scotia, with particular reference to his department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The fire which destroyed the Sydney pier was caused by certain welding operations carried on there, which ignited the oil carried in a
TMr. P. C. Black.]
fuel pipe running under the wharf. The fuel pipe ran through a tunnel inside the wharf, or under the wharf. That made it very difficult, of course, to get at the seat of the fire to extinguish it.
The great difficulty is that now and again we have complaints as to the cost of building. However, when we start to put up a proper type of building, that is a fireproof one, we are criticized for spending too much. As we see now, the wharf at Sydney undoubtedly would have been better had it been concrete, in the beginning. It would have cost more initially, of course, but in the long run we would have saved money. But we tried to get along and hoped we might get by with a wooden wharf. We did not succeed, unfortunately, in this instance.
The fire at Shelburne was caused by an overheated boiler in a building on the wharf.
There is no suspicion of sabotage in connection with any of the fires which occurred on the department's property?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.
Was there any insurance on any of these buildings, or is that in line with the department's policy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There was no insurance. The policy of the dominion government is not to insure buildings, on the theory that by spreading the risk among a great many buildings they save money by not insuring.
