5. Personnel supplies and services:	Food,
medical and dental stores, clothing and personal equipment, $27,846,280.

I have before me the recommendations made by the national health survey and tabled by the Minister of National Defence a few days ago. It is stated here that the ratio for medical officers per 1,000 troops in the army in Canada is 4-98, whereas overseas it is 3-83. In the entire service in the army, in Canada and overseas, the ratio is 4-5 per 1,000.
In the navy the ratio is 4-9, and in the air force it is 3-66. The report says:
In order to properly assess these ratios, it is necessary to study carefully the factors appearing in the appended tables. The air force has perhaps the least complex organization; it has also the lowest ratio. Many medical officers in all the services find their work less onerous than work which they had been accustomed to in civil practice. In the short time at the disposal of the committee it was not possible to study this subject exhaustively, and we did not feel competent to make any arbitrary

War Appropriation-Naval Services
recommendation. The committee is, however, of the opinion that a ratio of 3-5 to 3-7 per thousand should provide ample room for all medical needs. This statement, however, must be interpreted broadly in the light of indeterminate overseas requirements.
Would the minister be in a position to illuminate this statement? We find that in the air force the ratio is 3-66, and it is pointed out that they have the least complex organization. Could the minister give some explanation as to why the ratio in the navy and the army appears to be a good deal higher than in the other service?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: What is my hon. friend quoting from?
From the report tabled on Monday by the Minister of National Defence, containing the recommendations of the Canadian medical procurement and assignment board.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
would have to consult the medical people about that. I should think, however, that one factor which would serve to bring up the navy's average would be this: If you send a doctor to sea on a corvette, a frigate or a destroyer, with a personnel of 100, or 200 at the most, obviously the average would be raised. -But we have to do that in many cases. If all our men were on land, as they are in the air force and the army, it would be a different story. But we have small detachments at sea, in small ships. While all ships do not have doctors, yet a good many of them have. I fancy that would put the navy in a somewhat different position. However, that is just my own view, and I shall have to consult the medical people to see if there is any further statement to be made.

Another paragraph
states:
Army tables indicate the small amount of inter-service hospitalization which exists as between the navy, army and air force. It is felt that inter-service hospitalization should be encouraged wherever possible. This would relieve the burden carried by Department of Pensions and National Health hospitals and would promote interlocking of service medical facilities.
I have not had an opportunity to study in detail this very long and interesting report. Could the minister make a statement as to the possibility of having more extensive cooperation between the medical services of the army, the air force and the navy. For example, in large centres like Halifax, Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver it seems to me,, a layman, that greater cooperation might result in the conservation of medical personnel, and also in providing a more complete hospital service for those who are admitted.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
shall look into that again, along with the other question my hon. friend raised. But I may say there is a great deal of cooperation now. We are building a hospital at St. Hyacinthe, where we have a large naval establishment. But from there to the west coast we have no hospitals of our own. We have to use either civilian hospitals or hospitals of the other services. Where we have a hospital, such as that at'Halifax, I think we do work for the other services, as well. They possibly do the same for us. Similarly, at St. John's, Newfoundland, where we have a large naval hospital, the same would apply. However, I shall be glad to get the opinion of the medical branch on that point, and give my hon. friend an answer later.

I have one further question I should like to ask. Section 32 in the report states:
The whole picture presented as a result of this survey would have been more complete if information as to medical organization and the utilization of medical personnel overseas had been before us. The committee has not had time to secure information on the latest medical organization plans of the united nations. It is thought that these nations must have learned much by experience that would be of value in Canadian training and administrative arrangements. It would be useful if someone acting on behalf of the medical services in Canada could make an active endeavour to secure full information 'as to the medical organization in the united nations and their programmes and procedures.
It seems to me a pity that this matter did not receive consideration before the report came in. I wonder if the minister would consult his officers and see whether in the near future this recommendation might fee given consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
would rather do that.

The matter about which I have to speak, very briefly, has to do with the medical services not only of the navy but of all the armed forces of Canada. On previous occasions when the resolutions with reference to the war appropriations of the armed services were up for consideration I made observations with reference to promoting an amalgamation of the medical services in the three divisions. For reasons best known to the government, the recommendations which were made were not followed. But in the very document from which the last speaker has been quoting, namely, the report of the procurement and assignment board, the position which I took has been vindicated. I bring that to the attention of the minister in the hope that

War Appropriation-Naval Services
the recommendation which I make at this time may receive more favourable consideration than did former recommendations.
I have no doubt that when the European war is over and Canada is called upon to take part in the Pacific war, our naval services will be engaged in the southern Pacific. Our air forces and our land forces may also be engaged there. I wonder if information could be secured with reference to what tropical diseases any force which we might send to the Pacific theatre of war might face. The suggestion I am going to make is that we have sufficient personnel in the medical services of the armed forces of this country, and some of them might take time now to become somewhat proficient in the treatment of tropical diseases. The information which I have been able to gather, both through medical journals and through newspapers, is to the effect that the Japanese in the present war are suffering more casualties by virtue of. tropical diseases than they actually are from bullets. If such be the case, one can easily visualize the difficulties which any Canadian forces might have if they go to that particular theatre of war.
In any of the medical schools in this country tropical diseases are not studied to any extent. It might be of interest to the minister to know that the British government maintains a school in London for the study of tropical diseases. The United States government also maintains a school, which I think is at present situated at New Orleans, for the study of tropical diseases. Men who study medicine in this country and practise here have no occasion to come in contact with any of these diseases, and by virtue of that fact they are not conversant either with the diagnosis or with the treatment of tropical diseases.
The suggestion which I have to make to the minister is this, that he confer with his colleagues the Minister of National Defence for Air and the Minister of National Defence proper, with a view to taking fifty men from each of these services and making arrangements with the authorities either in the United States or in Great Britain that these men could go and take a four or a six months course in the study of tropical diseases, so that when our armed forces come to operate in the Pacific we shall have men in our navy, army and air medical services who will be conversant _ with tropical diseases, as to both diagnosis and treatment. It woiild be money and time well spent, and if it is a fact that there are some casualties from these diseases what I have suggested would certainly be of great benefit to the men in the armed forces. fMr. McCann.]
Tropical diseases are treated by specific types of drugs. I wonder if provision has been made for obtaining as much as possible of these drugs. For instance, there is only one specific drug-quinine-and a new synthetic drug, made for the treatment of malaria. I had occasion a year ago last fall to be in St. Louis at the convention of the American Public Health Association. St. Louis is the distributing centre for all the services of the United States as far as ordnance and supplies go. I was shown there $50,000,000 worth of quinine and opium which had been bought up by the United States government and stored there. While we have nothing like that amount, I wonder if there has been any bank of drugs procured and stored to be used for the forces in the event that these drugs are needed.
I would ask the minister to take up this suggestion with his colleagues, particularly with the directing forces of the medical forces in the various departments, and to give at least some consideration to a suggestion which I feel will prove of practical value in the event of Canada entering the Pacific war.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am glad to hear my hon. friend speak on that subject, and I am happy to be able to tell him and the committee that for some time certain naval medical officers have been giving study to the matter of tropical diseases. As a matter of fact, one of the naval medical officers to join early in the war was a man from western Canada who was in London at the outbreak of the war, studying tropical diseases. He attached himself to the Canadian navy then, and is still with us. Since then a good many others-I do not know just how many, but I will look into it-have taken up the study of tropical diseases. I should be very glad to carry out my hon. friend's suggestion of talking over this whole matter with the other two service ministers and cooperating with them in what is and what will be, I am sure, a very important branch of medical work.

Now that the public is taking so much more intelligent a view with regard to the prevention of venereal disease, would the minister tell the committee what steps are being taken in the navy to battle with it, and to what extent they have been attended by success?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
In a general way I can only tell my hon. friend that I think every effort is being made, but perhaps I should let that question stand and get a more detailed answer from the medical authorities to-morrow. I know that they, in

War Appropriation-Naval Services
common with all service medical authorities, are bending every effort to prevent the occurrence of this disease, but as to the exact details of what they are doing, I should like to get information from the doctors themselves.

I should be glad if the minister would do that; and also, perhaps, he could describe how many of the Canadian ships carry medical officers and how treatment is carried on where necessary in the smaller ships on which there are no medical officers.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

I should like to ask the minister with respect to facilities at the different naval stations regarding testing for night vision, whether these facilities are available at different training bases, such as Stadacona, Cornwallis, Sydney and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I should assume that they are. I know that the navy is one of the pioneers, and that, under the direction of Doctor Best and others, great attention has been given to this matter of night blindness and night vision. I should assume that every establishment has adequate facilities. But that is another matter which I shall look up and get a story on from the medical officers.

I wish the minister would pay particular attention to the checking of Stadacona before long. I would also ask him with respect to the milk supply at Deep Brook. I understand that the milk requirements are largely obtained from condensed milk, canned milk, rather than milk in bulk. If that is correct, will the minister give the explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is correct. For the moment at any rate I understand that there is not enough milk available in that locality to supply the requirements of the camp, which is a large camp of nearly 7,000 men. Consequently it has been found necessary to resort to milk powder, and machines have been installed which reconstitute this powder into milk at the camp.
That would be much more expensive, I presume, than obtaining milk from the producers?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is impossible to obtain it from the producers.
I understand that preference is given to producers if they are able to provide the milk?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
If they could provide whole milk we would be 100-99*l
glad to take it, but Deep Brook is midway between two relatively small towns, Digby and Annapolis, Annapolis with a population of about 1,200 and Digby with perhaps a few hundred more. There is no large city near at hand, and the. only milk supply there, as I see it, would be from the farmers in the country around, and that has not proved at all adequate for the purpose.
Move the camp to British Columbia.
I have heard it reported that the Wrens do not get a new uniform until the old uniform has been worn almost threadbare. What is the policy on refitting and providing the Wrens with new uniforms?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I should hardly think my hon. friend's information would be correct. The policy with regard to clothing for men and women is that they are given a complete outfit of clothing when they join. Then the Wrens are given a special allowance of $15 when they join to provide themselves with knick-knacks of one kind or another; also $44 a year to provide themselves with clothing, and an additional allowance of $3 a quarter or $12 a year to provide themselves with toilet necessities and-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Accessories.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: - other articles of feminine apparel.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The men in the navy are treated not quite so well as the Wrens. The government does not issue clothing to the men, except in the first instance. After that, the man has to buy his own clothing. But he is given the money, $44 a year, with which to buy it. The Wrens are also given the $44 a year and the other sums I mentioned, $15 at the start, and S3 a quarter.
Mr. B.OSS (St. Paul's): What about clothing when they are discharged? Is the policy the same as for the army and the air force? Do they take their clothes with them?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We let them keep a uniform.

Is there any difference between the clothing allowance given to - men in the navy and that given to men in the army and the air force?

War Appropriation-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The clothing allowance on discharge is the same amount.
The same all the way through?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
6.	Signal and wireless equipment, line construction, et cetera, $19,759,334.

This item is three times as great as last year. Would the minister explain the reason for that? With regard to signal and wireless equipment, does the navy do as the other two services, request Munitions and Supply to do their purchasing, or does the navy buy their own equipment direct? Which ever case it is, will the minister tell the committee how much is obtained from Canadian manufacturers and how much is brought in from equipment manufacturers in other countries?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know that I can answer all my hon. friend's questions, but I can answer some. First of all, all this equipment is bought through Munitions and Supply, who do all the purchasing for the navy, as for the other departments. The reason for the increase is as follows: In the first place, orders which were placed a considerable time ago will come in for payment this year. Orders for this equipment have to be placed far in advance sometimes. Then, of course, new signalling and wireless equipment is constantly coming into use. More ships will be in service next year and that will add to the total cost.
Is the principal part of this amount for instruments?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The greater part of it would be for instruments of one kind and another on ships. To give my hon. friend one or two items, let us take corvettes. We estimate that the total cost will be $3,500,000 or thereabouts. That will include new wireless telegraph equipment and so on -R.D.F. as it is called-and maintenance thereof.
Does the minister mean all corvettes at present building?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: All our corvettes in commission. And so with other ships, minesweepers, cruisers, destroyers. The greater part of this item is, therefore, expenditures on ships.
Does the minister mean that the $3,500,000 is locked up in instruments in all the corvettes we possess?

(Kingston City):
That is right. That is what we estimate 'for this year.
For this year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is what we estimate it will cost this year for this pui-pose. All this signal wireless, R.D.F., on corvettes alone will amount to nearly $3,500,000, and other ships proportionately. Then, of course, there is some of this, a relatively minor amount, for use at bases, radio stations, and training establishments.

Will the minister tell us more definitely the Reasons why this item is nearly five times as much this year as last year? It was $4,500,000 last year and this year S19,759,000, which is between four and five times as much, while the requisition for purchase and construction of ships is only about half as much.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This does not apply merely to new ships. I may say that therq is probably no field of naval warfare to-day in which there are so many changes as in this very matter of wireless equipment of one kind or another. It is not merely the sending of messages from one ship to another or from ship to shore; there is a great variety of ways in which radio and wireless can be used for detection purposes and purposes of communication. It is not simply new ships coming into commission this year that have to be equipped. Old ships have to have their equipment renewed or modern equipment installed; and, as I pointed out to the hon. member for Yale, we find this year that a considerable number of orders, placed some time ago, are coming for payment. Goods are being delivered this year and payment must be made? In connection with some of it, a relatively minor amount, the increase is on account of increased facilities at bases where we have training establishments. Generally, I think I can say that the great bulk of the increase is owing to the necessity of having modern equipment on both old and new ships.

May I ask the minister whether the land line being constructed at Aldergrove by a private company is being built by the company on behalf of the Department of National Defence for Naval Services? My impression is that it was being built under contract by a private company for the minister's department. Second, in regard

War Appropriation-Naval Services
to the changing over of these miniature carriers, in connection with signalling equipment, is that under the minister's department or under the Department of Munitions and Supply? There are several carriers at Vancouver.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is a British commitment.
Will the minister look up the question to-morrow with reference to the line construction to ascertain whether it belongs to his department or the private company?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend means that the construction work was undertaken by a private company for us.
That is what I wish to know.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I should think that is almost certainly the case.
The line will belong to the minister's department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.
Will the minister tell us what part of this item is wanted for land-line construction and -where this work is being done?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Landline and teletype and morse contracts amount to about 81,000,000. There is another item of about 81,000,000 for new land-line construction.
Are any of the land lines being built on Cape Breton island, where they have had antiquated sendees?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This deals with lines between, for instance, Ottawa and New York, or Halifax and Louisburg. What my hon. friend refers to is covered under a joint service arrangement with the army and the air force. That is, the provision, of telephone lines in remote parts of the country. That is under another item.
Under another item in the minister's estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is an item here for the Atlantic command project, $250,000. I fancy the land lines my hon. friend has in mind would be covered by that.

Does the minister care to give information as to whether the lines serving the northern part of New Brunswick, going into the gulf of St. Lawrence,
and performing a very useful function, are being renovated? Perhaps he would give us that information later?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

I have a few questions I should like to ask.
Item stands.
